utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. So there are no remaining doubts, I have to emphasise in the beginning that once again our procedure follows the Rules as laid down in order to the depositions to be taken pursuant to Rule 71 under Rule 15 bis the order of 11 September, 2002, due to the continued illness of Judge Fassi Fihri. We started yesterday, came to a certain point when the witness was kind enough to read out some portions of earlier notes, but before we start, please let us know in what case we are acting today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Become, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any obstacles starting immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not on our side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, thank you very much for reading those notes regarding your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic. Did you complete reading those notes yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did we complete the reading of what was in the-- yes, we did. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We noted at several points you said "something". Did that indicate that you could not today read the word that you had written six and a half years ago?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that under the circumstances yesterday, and there were circumstances which led to a stuttered rendering for which I apologise to Your Honours, that I was not able to recognise the word at the pace at which I wish to proceed, and I have not seen those notes for several years and was not aware that they would be introduced. That's what I meant by "something". And there were also other distractions which I can explain if the Court wishes, particularly on the pages themselves. There was an unfortunate circumstance in the actual document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you'd like to explain that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, yes, if I may. If it please the Court, and I don't wish to -- just pertaining to and I would certainly be very happy to answer any questions on that reading and anything that would help the Court, but I didn't know I was going to have to read them. I certainly stand by them. But when I was asked by telephone sometime back to have them declassified by a previous Bench, I was guaranteed that any addresses or telephone numbers on the page would be deleted. It's my fault that I didn't notice an address when I was looking through them quickly to have them cleared yesterday, but a sensitive address had turned out had not been deleted and when I saw it on the page I was rather thrown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you now and at a later time we'll go into closed session and take care of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. And there were also some distractions in the courtroom which put me off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to go over a couple of quick points on the notes you took. Again, you indicated you did not write the questions. Do you attempt to write word-for-word? Is this a transcript of a conversation or is it notes you took during a conversation getting the substance of what was said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not claim it to be an exact transcript of every word spoken. Shorthand goes up to 150 words a minute which is faster than most people speak. A hundred and ten or so words is average. I can write somewhere around 90, I think. So it's not an exact transcript of what is said, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, what you are hearing is what the interpreter is giving you rather than understanding the language of the speaker, Dr. Kovacevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It's -- it is -- it is a rendering of a translation, and it's normal practice to go over it with the translator afterwards, which we did on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also another colleague taking notes as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Cohen from the Times?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on later that day. Later that day, did you interview Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it that that interview took place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in what I understood to be the office or his office of a day health centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present during your interview with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Cohen, as mentioned before, the translator, Dr. Stakic, and another man who was introduced some way through the conversation as a Mr. Kondic, variously presented as his deputy at the health centre initially and thereafter as his lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us to the best of your recollection now the approximate time of day that the interview took place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate of how long you talked to Dr. Stakic in his office?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as long as with Dr. Kovacevic. I would say about -- between maybe an hour, hour and a half maximum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that conversation, did Dr. Stakic indicate what his present position was? Or before you actually interviewed him, there was any communication with him regarding any position, political position he held at that time, February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had, of course, been the mayor previously, and I knew that, but there was, yes, a conversation about his candidacy to become the mayor again for the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to read the notes of the interview with Dr. Stakic. If they could be provided to the witness. And again, before we begin, perhaps you can review these to see if there is any confidential material that you do not want to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the procedure of yesterday, we should continue with DP6 and starting with the first page DP6-1. Could the usher be so kind and during the reading out of the document provide always the page just to be read out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are certainly all right for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They aren't distributed, I take it and therefore, could you indicate to the usher is it the correct side to start with which you can see now on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then DP -- it's now to be read out, DP6-1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may begin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [As read] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. At the top, "Stakic". Some lines which I don't think from looking at the page are attributable to him. They come above a line below which appears his name again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. May I ask you when you're reading as you just began to do indicate at any time if there is a speaker other than Dr. Stakic that you are recording. If we do not hear you identify any other speaker, we will assume that the text is what you're recording that Dr. Stakic said.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. And certainly. Obviously if Your Honours aren't happy with the labelling of the notes, then please tell me. The name "Stakic" at the top of the page. Somebody else now speaking, it seems. He left here in 19 -- it looks like 1983. It's a short period which, arrow, which only a short -- our candidate for the something for a Croatian family. Line. Not Stakic but S-T-K-I-C, arrow pointing down to text. Dr. Stakic now speaking. I hope that the peace will last. I can talk about my work here and the lack of medicine. Entered politics in 1990. Try and make a solution for doctors in private practice. That is when I went into politics. In the former Yugoslavia, there was not, sorry, It was not -- pardon me. In former Yugoslavia, there was not a possibility for doctors to practice privately. What happened later, I didn't have anything to do with, that is why I turned back. I am still a member of the local parliament. I saw that I cannot work on both sides, so I resigned from, couldn't do my work and hold office. In the margin, sometimes bulldog like. It's not Dr. Stakic talking, it's a note. There's a question and I can't read it. Objectives or objections something. Questions. When dire or direction or something will come back in there -- will come back on the theme. Talk about the lack of medicine. Humanitarian organisations coming here and bringing medicines. I am a candidate for the city mayor. This territory is very interesting because Mr. Roy Gutman got a Pulitzer. He was here a couple of times. Drank together. And he went away and wrote a lot of lies about what was happening here. He was paid to do that. Note in the margin, not Mr. Stakic talking. Swivels in chair, deep in thought. Was working or taking medicines in. Arrow -- an arrow usually implies -- I'm sorry, it's not Dr. Stakic speaking, this is me. An arrow usually implies -- it points towards my colleague. He's sitting on my right. Wouldn't, cannot, or something cannot the medicines in. Hundred and fifty kilometres. Instead only 60. In this century, three wars happened here. These two world wars -- there were two world wars, but included that was a civil war which happened here. If democratic west really wants peace in these territories, they should accept this status today, a Bosnia of two independent units. If Serbs with 500.000 expelled from Croatia and many Serbs from there who lost their territories, and they accepted IFOR. That is the only real solution, Bosnia, Czechoslovakia, Cyprus. If we - turn the page - cannot live as brothers, we can live as good neighbours. If we recognised Bosnia with cantons in 1991, we would have missed the war. Now, after the war we cannot go back. This is the reality. In the margin I have written "Uneasy," and another word. As a doctor I saw many wounded persons, mute, killed persons without parts of the body or of body. I cannot say that any problems were solved by war. We watched the Muslim-Croatian federation television. Alija Izetbegovic, every Muslim should have a gun. Now have a peace signed. And he said, this is the first spec. The first part, he said. I am not scared -- excuse me -- I am not scared, but we expect a reaction of the democratic west. Alija Izetbegovic is not yet declared a war criminal. If we -- if you had an Alija on the same level of as our president, he should be accused. If our president is accused, crossed out, Alija should be accused before our president, because he was a president of state. Karadzic was the president of the SDS party. He is much more responsibility. One and a half million Serbs, arrow pointing right. It was the same feeling as if the USA would break up and you had a line -- you had to live in another state. I saw and I expect the West to react, but I saw what happened -- but I saw what was happening. The same things as in the Second World War. They had bombs, got, had aeroplanes. My great-grandfather mobilised by the Austria-Hungarian Empire. He was sent to attack Serbia along with Tito. Getting Serbs or the Serbs, they were first opposed, and they went into Serbia. Was on the English side. He stayed alive and came to live here. Died in 1981 when I was only 18. 1941, my grandfather was in the Partisans. He was not a communist, he was killed fighting the Ustashas, 1944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes DP6-2 and now follows -3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now in the war again, my father was against the Muslims and Croatians, have done more evil to the Serbs than the Germans along with the protection of the NDH. When the people saw the Croatian flag in 1991, the same flag as the Ustashas and the speeches of Franjo Tudjman, it recalled Croatia of the Second World War. Created in Canada, the Serbs were expelled in their constitution. The police and soldiers were sent to - something - or in Serbian territory. The question for us is: Do the Serbs have to stay on their knees or go back to Jasenovac a second time? It had to be if it happened. The international community established new borders, and that way we want to have peace. Don't is doing -- Dayton is doing to put Bosnia, America, England, and France and think politics of. War started in Croatia. The reaction was not too much. All we wanted to do was to live the way we had always lived. Arrow pointing right. There were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps. As a journalist you have to come on the spot. They were never collected. Omarska --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. This last sentence beginning there were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps, do you know what he was referring to from the context, total context of the conversation and questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. We asked him and his friend about Omarska, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And about the pictures, specifically the television pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you want to add something in this context, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I will. Well, this -- at this point, as I've just said, he and his friend are asked about Omarska and the -- and there is a conversation that ensues, and specifically about the television pictures of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned several times his friends, and I know that you gave a qualification, being neutral, as his friend. Would you once again try to the best of your recollection, tell us what was the capacity of this friend? Only what you know quite sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to answer your question. I was myself a little confused, however. He was at first introduced as the deputy -- as Dr. Stakic's deputy running the health centre. Then as my notes will later note, I think, he was introduced as his lawyer. And then afterwards, and this is slightly jumping ahead but I have to to answer your question properly, the -- well, somebody said that actually neither of these were true and this man was actually part of the police or security forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm asking right now because to a certain extent it is important. When taking these notes, at that point in time you had which impression, friend, lawyer, or the said capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point in the notes, he's the deputy head of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. There were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps. As a journalist, you have to come on the spot. They were never collected. Omarska. There was only interrogation process for particular number of Muslims, and when they established a new prison, that was only a place where the Muslims had illegal weapons, during the war in this region. If I could interrupt myself here to -- in accordance with your request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's now a question, as I recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me if I may, Your Honour. Excuse me, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the process. If there is a question pending the witness can answer it. The witness is required, as we did with yesterday's reading of his notes, first to read the notes. After that the OTP can gladly or any one of us can gladly inquire if there is any inconsistency or issues that aren't clear, because quite frankly the last comment that Mr. Vulliamy made is inconsistent with the typewritten transcript or the typewritten notes that we've received, and I think this would be better in order to keep a clear record that we at least have the totality of the notes as he may recall them or as he may read them to us today and then we can go back. And again it's not an issue of extending it I just think it would make for a clearer record and when we come back to the points because they are critical points obviously. So I would ask that it be read, and if necessary we go back and question him on things that are perhaps vague or inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt this is the most appropriate way to proceed, but please look at page 10, line 22. There it reads: "If I could interrupt myself" and I think it's for the witness, when quoting his own notes, that he can -- may give additional explanations. Please proceed in this way therefore. I think we should refrain from interrupting the witness during reading out these notes, but nevertheless, whenever you have additional spontaneous recollection, please don't hesitate to tell us what comes into your mind when reading out this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to accommodate everyone and make it clear when I'm to label when I'm departing from the page if you follow me, which I will do now. This is now me talking. As I recall, there is now a question about -- some sort of question about bringing in the Jasenovac camp as contrasted to or compared to Omarska. The -- now I am reading from the page: The comparison is not good. The Muslims in Omarska had food, doctors. They didn't work. It was not a hotel, but the comparison, comp., with a concentration camp is not right. It was not a concentration camp. Omarska was not a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's now -- sorry. Orthodox is the mind of the world. Me speaking now. There are now two lines written by somebody else. Pravoslavlje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can explain. Point to the two lines you're referring to and tell us who actually wrote that on the page.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This and this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating the area boxed, the two lines boxed in the upper left.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a star to the left. That is somebody else's hand. To the best of my recollection, it is Mr. Kondic, the thus far deputy of the health centre. Pravoslavlje, Pravo e Slavan. Now, the Serbs go to extreme only when their freedom is threatened. Puts on a tape. It's the last cassette I bought as a student. Fiddles about with a tape. Arrow down. Nashville skyline. Me speaking: Over to the side of the page in a margin down from the top. Back to the text. This text goes off the page, so what I say now might not be the complete note. It's not so present something. The Serbs want to - something - free. Unfortunately, they learned to defend - off the page - freedom even in - off the page - Jasenovac. You - off the page - cannot make a pic. Picture of the Serbs in their - off the page - freedom is in their something - off the page - psych., psychology. Freedom is holy to the Serbs. Also our Orthodox, crossed out, our just and true religion. Serbs are not extreme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt for a moment. That paragraph that you just read something that "is not so something present," I believe you were reading the text to the right of the page; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the speaker is on that text?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the other gentleman that is not Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could now proceed. Indicate who the next speaker is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now back to Dr. Stakic in the main page. Reading from the text. Two hundred and ninety patients, 15.000. 107 new TB patients. Children don't have - something - in schools. They don't have books. After school, they don't have opportunities for other actions. What shall we do with children from early ages? What shall we do with them? If we did not have ICRC or MSF, 70 per cent of our needs, medical materials, what will happen? Sanctions are get alive or something alive. Our economy doesn't work. Fifteen to 30 per cent. And can I say Chinese saying: Don't give up hope. Take me to work. Let us live and work. Tues. 21. Most don't even work. We can only defend ourselves. No one can stop us from defending. If the west allow the west attacked. Arrow pointing to the right. At this moment, the place of city mayor is free. SDS party has a right to have a new candidate which are I or I am eyeing, crossed out. We taught the German Empire how to eat with a spoon and now we have to learn and they want to teach us about democracy. Socialist Party and Republika Srpska. And they -- and they - something - they are independent party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something dep. part or dep. party will decide who will be or who will - something, something - it was succeed or success to be close to Sarajevo. Stakic: The Serb or Serbs are not scared. Jasenovac is our sacred thing. These days, Tudjman wants to establish Jasenovac as a monument to the Croatian victims, to put the same between victims and killers. The time will come when we will have a great victory in this area. End text. Back up to the top of the page, quoting from the margin: Man: It's not possible to solve this problem without the Serbs. We will be more slow, will be more slow, but the Serbs can wait. It's necessary to wait for freedom and to fight for freedom. We used all democratic ways to keep freedom, but we couldn't. If you spent a bit more time -- or sorry, if you spent a little bit more time with us, it could be clear for -- for you that the Serbs did not begin this war and all this killing in the camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt again. That passage that you just read, you said you were quote from the margin, "It's not possible to solve this problem," who was the speaker for that passage you've just read?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That passage I've just read was not Dr. Stakic. It was Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you completed the reading?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the margin, yes. Now we go back to the main text, Dr. Stakic speaking, quoting: IFOR. Both had a -- something had to be -- to something in this territory or these territories. This is the -- this is the something hour, we. When the Serbs fight for four years and there are no compunctions or something, com something, within they. There are no Krajina Serbs, no Bosnian Serbs, or Serbian Serbs, only Serbs. Karadzic only thinks about Serbs. GP specialising physiotherapy. Stopped specialising because of the war. Now I hope I will finish. During the war, offer in P. Neuropsychiatrists, not like Karadzic, because people went into politics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: New page. He said the Serbs were mad people. It's not a good idea. Vietnam syndrome. That's his lawyer, arrow pointing to the right. If IFOR became upkeep, cannot -- myself talking, cannot read this next bit, photocopy too light. We don't want to go to Sarajevo. I don't miss it. If we have to -- oh. If we have the place, then -- then let them come back, but first we have to settle the Serbs. When a man did to make fire first or for, and the photocopy is too light, time in history, if you did store or stone in the -- it's not for people, it's many -- it means something else. We don't think Prijedor is any different from any other city, because Izetbegovic is making. Vinko Kondic. Arrow pointing to text in a box. Kondic speaking: You have to ask Izetbegovic why. Izetbegovic is making a negative city, negative city of Prijedor. That is why he wants to win again. He got advice from someone. Back to the -- me talking. Back to the main page. Dr. Stakic talking: The same -- some -- I can't read that -- permission for credit. The same -- some permission for credit from the west. We will make a new Petrovac, new Drvar. There are nine reception centres, 2.000 refugees. They didn't have homes with roofs. The Serbs from Omarska. When NATO bombed, was -- that was int. for something. NATO, arrow, shelled this area. Fifteen to 18 refugees in one house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you think that we don't have pain in that village Kozarac? We found 3.500 automatic guns. For whom were they supposed to work? It's very clear that these guns were intended for Serbs, not for hunting Serbs, not for hunting animals. There was a list from the SDA party, a list of who got number of guns. Something -- number of military units. DB, state security police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this special effort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a pleasure, Your Honour, thank you, if it helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Mr. Vulliamy: Did you ask Dr. Stakic about the houses that were destroyed along the roads, particularly along the roads of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did, but I think my colleague did, specifically about the houses along -- well, along the road of -- in that road in Kozarac and in the village of Kozarac itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said at one point, and I'm referring to at -- I believe it's 10:03:12, NATO bombed, do you know in what context Dr. Stakic said this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I imagine we must have been talking about the bombing of September 1995. The bombing that ended the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that was at the same time you asked him about the destruction of the houses along the road to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been but the shorthand isn't clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you review that section of your notes, look at it a second time, and if you have any further insight or not, that's fine. I believe that would be on DP6-6.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last three lines, several lines.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion of NATO and the bombing of which I have -- I mean, it's not a complete sentence, it's just some notes of the conversation does immediately precede the passage on Kozarac. I recall there is a question of some kind which is, you know -- he says, "Do you think we don't feel pain?" I think the question may have been, "Do you feel any pain when you see the houses burnt out along the road," but it's not marked in front of me here. But that -- I mean, the conversation about Kozarac follows on immediately from that about the NATO bombing certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are connected in that way at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing for the translation. You indicated Dr. Stakic said at one time that the television pictures were pictures of Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps and it was in the context of that the television pictures of Omarska on the visit in which you were present.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt in my mind or that of my colleague, and I don't think there was any doubt in his mind that we were talking about the pictures that were taken in the Omarska camp during my visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you introduce yourself to Dr. Stakic in 1996 as one of the journalists who had been present and had visited the camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that it was evening when you visited Dr. Stakic. Do you recall Dr. Stakic making any remark concerning the time of day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and my colleague and I discussed this afterwards as we left because we were told something to the effect of "It's brave of you to be around here at this time of night," and an ominous remark made about journalists in the area at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be clear, who made that remark?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic. I think Mr. Kondic made a remark as well. I think it was -- it was -- we were told by both of them that it was time to go soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to play a short video back to 1992 and your visit. We talked about the women in the line, and I'd like you to view the following. It's about a minute and a half video. Tell us if you recognise -- this is a new video. It's taken from ERN number V0000662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It may be of assistance if we could have present documents Exhibit S2 and S3 just in case it can assist the witness. It may be put on the ELMO only later, after we have seen the video clip. Thank you. And may I, in the meantime, ask the representative of the Prosecutor's office, please, in order not to create too much confusion, do we have available the same video we had yesterday that we could rewind to this point where we saw in the video on this lining up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. It might be helpful because it may be taken on different occasions and, therefore, it should be available, please, immediately after this video. You got the message? Thank you. Please proceed with the video prepared for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise the woman in the right foreground of the video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Unless it's the ITN -- no. She didn't look like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a producer type of person with ITN?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a sort of PA lady who usually wore sunglasses, which she isn't here. If it's her, it's not a very flattering -- I mean, I don't recognise her, but I think it might be her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just stop for a moment, please. Can you identify the building to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the police headquarters in -- in, so far as I recognise it, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And once again to the best of your recollection, this is close or opposed to the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's across the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Across the road. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's the end of the tape, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you recognise when she turned towards the camera the woman I asked you about earlier?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the ITN lady, yes. She's got her sunglasses above her head. If I can help -- I'm trying to help as much as I can. I think that maybe one of the entrances shown might be the civic centre itself, actually, if not the building across the road. But this is without a doubt in the same complex, on a square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another quick question. Go back to 1992, you talked about the battle that you believe was staged on your trip from the Municipal Assembly building --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- To the Omarska camp. You said that there was a 20-minute or so delay while the people from what you called the Crisis Committee conferred for you to get information to leave. Where that battle took place was that before the turn-off to the Omarska camp where you saw the sign or after the turn-off to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the turn-off to the Omarska camp, because the -- the main road leaves Prijedor, and the Omarska turn-off is -- I wouldn't want to be -- I mean, it's roughly four to five miles down the road. And we went past it and then turned off to the right towards Omarska on a series of, as I said yesterday, I think, minor roads, or very minor roads, and that's where this so-called exchange of fire, this what I called a prank took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned and went and visited at least the gate of the Omarska camp in 1996, did you take the turn-off that you had gone past in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a more direct route to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely. It was a short distance to the front gate down from that turn-off, yes, and it was all paved road, properly paved road, with a sort of a bridge before you get to the maintenance to the camp which is very clearly marked Rudnik Omarska, Omarska Mine. We did not go through that gate in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence is prepared to start the cross-examination immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please proceed until five minutes past 11. Cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just pause and have the usher lower the ELMO a little bit.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thanks. Yes, that would be better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions this morning in regard to your direct examination and some of the missions you had in 1991 through 1996 in Bosnia as well as Croatia in the former Yugoslavia. As before, since you and I have had an opportunity to have an exchange --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down and repeat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and I have had an opportunity to discuss matters in connection with Prijedor actually four years ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same rules apply as they did then. I'll be asking the questions and if you can wait and give us your honest and thoughtful answer as you have during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If at any time, sir, you don't understand my question, please ask me to clarify and I'll attempt to do my best to clarify the question so that you may fully understand it and give us a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you for the guidance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a little bit about your background. I know that you have a degree which I think you've identified as a PPE in politics, philosophy, and economics; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that you do not have any military background or military expertise?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In service, no. Of warfare, obviously yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, also that you have no background in criminal justice or any police-type work?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, the interpreters are asking kindly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, also that you have no political background or experience?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been interested in politics, but I've never been -- I was briefly -- as a student I was a member of the Labour Party which is the party of government in Britain, but I've never been -- held political office of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you're not a lawyer, are you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, are you a demographer?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A demographer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a demographer, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you in preparation for your testimony here in the Stakic matter, did you review any demographic reports or data in connection with the Prijedor municipality relating to the period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically in connection to any preparation for this case, no, but in -- obviously in my coverage of the war, I had some idea of how -- of the demographic make-up of the area, yes, and of course how it changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, what is it that you reviewed prior to testifying yesterday and today? What materials did you review?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pertaining to the demography of Prijedor prior --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pertaining to the case of the OTP versus Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I review. I reviewed the shorthand notes that I have read out this morning, and I reviewed the -- well, I say I reviewed. I read very quickly some typewritten notes that I compiled with the -- my colleague and with -- on the basis of conversation with him and the translator, and I had a look at some of but not all of because there's a lot of it, our previous appointment here in the case of Dr. Kovacevic. But my actual preparation has been -- I mean -- sorry, if it's relevant, but it's been a very busy week in New York and I have not had an enormous amount of time to prepare specifically, but I'm certainly happy to answer any questions about Prijedor and demography because I obviously studied that earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't limit it just to demography, but my question is this: In preparation for your testimony here, have you had an opportunity to review your testimony in the Dusko Tadic case wherein you testified on or about June 6th through 7th of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had -- I've looked at some of it, yes. To be honest, I haven't had time to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to preface your comments by telling me you're honest. I presume all your answers will be honest and truthful, okay?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, have an opportunity to review prior to your testimony here in this matter the testimony you gave on April 24th, 1998, which was the OTP against General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't looked at that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, and I think you told us that, in part review the testimony you gave from July 15th through July 18th, 1998, in the OTP versus Dr. Kovacevic case?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact dates but I've had a chance to look at some of that testimony but I haven't read it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, have an opportunity to review your testimony of last year, June 1, 2001, in the OTP versus Sikirica case or otherwise known as the Keraterm case?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen my testimony in that case. It was, as I recall, very brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your preparation for testifying here did you have the opportunity to review the statement that you gave to the ICTY on or about March 25th through 28th, 1997?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you help me with what that was about? I think the answer is no but just in case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- a statement. Is that in Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether you ever gave a statement to representatives of the ICTY in connection with trials that may be proceeding before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've given statements to the Tribunal before, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interviewed in the fall of 1995 in the case of Tadic. I gave a statement at some date - I don't recall exactly when it was - in the case of General Blaskic, and I was called to testify also in the case of Dr. Kovacevic, but I'm not sure which one you're referring to at the moment, and I did not give a statement in the case of the Keraterm which you mentioned. I was called by the Defence, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg to differ with you on that, sir, because I was in that case and you were actually called by the Prosecutor. And the Defence, one limited defendant had an opportunity to cross-examine you last year on June 2001. But be that as it may, I'm sure we could get a stipulation from --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would be happy to stipulate that the witness was called subject to 92 bis subject only to cross-examination by the Defence and redirect by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, sir, known a gentleman by the name of Robert Donia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as a foreign correspondent, can you describe for me what your duties were in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- in 1992, the war in Croatia was recently over, and I went back after the agreement that ended that war to try and continue my -- my duties in Italy, working mostly on the Mafia, and corruption scandals at that time. And then the conflict in Bosnia began. I was briefly in Sarajevo, but my duties began really with the assignment that I described yesterday, and I would call that my first real engagement or assignment and -- in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And from then on, my duties were to form part of a roster covering that conflict, which later developed into, as it were, a sort of branch conflict between the government army and Croatian forces, Bosnian Croatian forces, and my duties were to form part of that roster and to try as best I could to service the newspaper from Italy, which I didn't do very much for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right and I understand that. Thank you. My question really as I asked you four years ago, your duty as a journalist, sir, is to report the facts regardless of what assignment you are given; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your duties are not, sir, to distort the facts are they?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact it would be a violation of journalistic ethics, would it be?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would certainly not be very good reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't think it's a violation of ethics?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that a journalist should embellish facts those upon which he learns or obtains while on a mission, if you will?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you don't need to. Facts would speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it's not very good ethical practice. Bad ethical practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just go on with one more question on this ethical practice. Is it ethically appropriate or proper for a journalist to take quotes from one person and attribute it to another?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is not just a good idea?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a violation of everything that you were taught, all the training that you obtained and all the experience that you have as a journalist as a foreign correspondent, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a violation of those things, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you interview people as a journalist, do you have any duties and obligations to people that you're interviewing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are obligations. If you are told something is off the record, then you are obliged that it be off the record. That's as far as I would say. Otherwise, there are no hard and fast rules. You have obligations to write down, to the best your ability, what they say and to report it, certainly, but I'm not quite sure what you mean by duties -- when you interview -- in terms of introductions and stuff like that or what? I mean -- you say -- you're saying what are the obligations when you interview somebody. To record what they say and to publish it to the best your ability accurately and to -- and to put off the record things that are clearly labelled by the interviewee as being off the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there an obligation by a journalist, sir, to identify themselves to witnesses or potential defendants in a war crimes tribunal such as you -- when you interviewed Dr. Kovacevic, Dr. Stakic, Major Milutinovic, and Professor Koljevic in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if you feel that by doing so you're putting yourself in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall making that decision deliberately?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall thinking that it would not be advisable since I was in that territory without permission. I had had some bad experiences and did not feel that I was persona grata in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me understand this in connection with journalists. When you do an interview you keep what's known as contemporaneous notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those contemporaneous notes are then transformed into what's known as an aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not important but yes, if other reporters are present, then you'll match up the notes because as I explained earlier, what you will have on the page is not always an exact transcription of every word said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your aide-memoire it becomes into what is known as your published work; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes. Not always. It depends -- it depends on the circumstances. It depends on whether it's a press conference and there are 20 notebooks involved or it's -- it's -- sometimes, yes. Quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so you can be clear, Mr. Vulliamy, I'm pausing sometimes so the translation and the various languages can get complete.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not a hesitancy nor do I have any questions about your answers. Just so you know that the pause may be indicative of that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to put that in context. Contemporaneous notes, aide-memoirs, and the ultimate article. In fact, on August of 1992, specifically August 5th, when you visited the Omarska and Trnopolje camps, you shared with us that the following day immediately upon leaving Trnopolje went to Belgrade. The next day you wrote what essentially was an article that was ultimately published on August 7th, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the three items that we mentioned, contemporaneous notes, aide-memoirs and the article, do you consider any one more or less trustworthy or reliable?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long time since I saw the actual article. I would say that the notes were the more reliable, but the article might have things in it that perhaps in that case ITN had recorded or that my two colleagues who you saw on the television yesterday might have put in their books. So in that respect, the article could be more reliable inasmuch as I keep trying to stress that what you put in your book is the fastest you can or the best you can write stuff down. If there are two or three of you and there's an interpreter, you will go over the stuff. So in that respect, the article could be closer to what is actually intended to be said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me switch to the February 1996 meeting that you had with Dr. Kovacevic, Dr. Stakic, and I think also Major Milutinovic, as well as Professor Koljevic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met all those gentlemen, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness could also be asked to pause before he answers so the interpreters can catch up and also so that two speakers do not interrupt each other. So if you could just pause, Mr. Vulliamy, a few seconds after the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Certainly. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained or I thought I understood your testimony yesterday that you went back to the Prijedor area in order to do a follow-up story in connection with the events that transpired in August of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was part of the series I described that was commissioned in order to retrace some of the steps in the war after its conclusion at the Dayton Peace Accords, and it was with reference to that that I went. And of course this call to Prijedor, as I think should be clear, was with reference back to the -- I thought and I think other people thought to be the important day of August the 5th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, as you described previously in your testimony, it was part professional, part personal that you went back in February of 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so that I could have the context of the purpose for which you went to this February 1996 meeting, is it true, sir, that prior to that meeting you had met with the OTP trial attorney Mike Keegan who was the legal attorney against Dr. Kovacevic in his trial in 1998?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd been summoned to be a witness in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were summoned before February of 1996 to be a witness against Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that I was going to be a witness. I don't know quite what the -- or was likely to be a witness. Well, no. I can certainly help you with this. I was first interviewed in April 1995, long before, generally, and then sometime later that year I was told I would be a witness in the trial. So obviously I talked to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea that the indictment against Dr. Kovacevic was not public at that time in 1995 or 1996? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. A question --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know if there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First please. Now, I think it's necessary for me to recall. Slow down and wait and pause before question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I make an objection? The question is misleading. It says: "Are you aware that the indictment was not public?" In fact there was no indictment at that time. The indictment had not yet been written. So I think saying it was not public would be misleading to the witness and the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, if we look at the answer the witness gave, I think it was quite clear. He is under oath. He was well aware of what the OTP at that time was preparing and had completed whether privately or publicly, which is namely the indictment against Dr. Kovacevic, Simo Drljaca, and Dr. Milomir Stakic, which we have before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we don't have to go into further details. Your question was quite clear. You spoke about an indictment against Dr. Kovacevic, and we are all aware that at that point in time there was none, such an indictment, and therefore, please, may I ask you to be concrete and detailed in your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, in fact, in April of 1995, is it true that you were visited in your offices in Washington, DC by Michael Keegan, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And share with me so that I have it right, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he -- he said he was investigating the case of Dusko Tadic and wanted to hear from me because the case as reported to me, I'd never heard of Dusko Tadic then, focused on Omarska and Trnopolje, particularly Trnopolje, I believe, and he wanted to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he ask you, sir, that he wanted you to be possibly an expert witness for him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he asked me then. I think he might have done, but it wasn't confirmed in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for what reason -- and for what reason, sir, to the best of your recollection was it that Mr. Keegan wanted you to be an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, because the witness did not state Mr. Keegan wanted him to be expert witness. That's counsel's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Vulliamy, that in fact Mr. Keegan asked you to be an expert witness on the issues of widespread and systematic patterns in the Prijedor area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that that was my sort of label, if you like, the widespread and systematic thing. But I don't know when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that label?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it must have been the Prosecutors, the Prosecution. It was not a term that I was familiar with until I heard it during my -- during briefing for the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequent to the April 1995 meeting that you had --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Correction. I was aware of it academically but not in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to concentrate on the time period from April 1995 up until the time that you interviewed Dr. Stakic, among others. On how many occasions had you then met with the OTP or any of their representatives?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once certainly. I came over for what was their sort of the main consultation on the Tadic case. It was sometime during the fall or early winter of 1995. It was cold. That's my memory. And that was -- if I hadn't been told I was going to be a witness before in the Tadic case, I was told it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sometime in the fall of 1995. At any time from that period up until the time of February of 1996, had you met with the Office of the Prosecutor in connection with the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the meeting that I've just mentioned in the fall of 1995 did focus on the Prijedor area because the Tadic case focused on the -- on the camps. So that was when that we did talk about the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have those two meetings, the April 1995 meeting, the fall 1995 meeting, and my question to you, sir, is subsequent to that fall 1995 meeting, up until February 1996, had you had any contact, correspondence or communication with the OTP in connection with the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have spoken, but I don't -- can't remember when, with Mr. Keegan by phone, and I -- but I don't think I came to The Hague, pertaining to the Tadic case and also pertaining to a separate set of allegations being made about the Trnopolje camp, in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision for your editor to agree to send you back in the Bosnian area, Prijedor mainly, was made when again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around December 1996 it would have been just after the Dayton agreement. Around Christmas time, when we were planning the series.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean December 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I correct myself and you're absolutely right. 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It couldn't have been after the meeting, right? The decision to go back couldn't have been made after the events where you went there and interviewed the individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Thank you for the correction. December 1995, I said just after the Dayton Agreement which was signed, I think, in mid-December 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, sir, consult with members of the OTP to determine what questions you should ask of Dr. Kovacevic or Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't know I was going to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it your testimony, sir, that at no time Michael Keegan or any representatives from the OTP knew, despite having a meeting with them in April of 1995 and in the fall of 1995 and having telephone communication was then prior to February 1996, that you didn't tell Mr. Keegan that you were going to interview Dr. Kovacevic or Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, as you put it, tell Mr. Keegan I was going to interview those men, nor did he know I was going to interview those men, nor did I know that I was going to interview those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So immediately after your interview in February 1996, what you did, sir, was in fact you took your disk from your computer with a cover letter and you shipped it to Mr. Keegan; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did send a disk to Mr. Keegan because I thought that what we had come across in those interviews was extremely relevant to the case in which I was called. I was trying to help the Tribunal. The case I was called in to testify concentrated on Omarska and Trnopolje and what happened in the Prijedor area, and I presume they -- it would be of interest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you retain a copy of the letter or correspondence that accompanied the disk that you sent to Mr. Keegan immediately after the meeting you had in February of 1996 with, among others, Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have been, and I don't remember what it was, but it would have been little more than a card or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for my edification, do you have expertise on the issues relating to widespread and systematic patterns that may have occurred in or around the Prijedor area in 1992, May through September?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Irrelevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I wouldn't say irrelevant to this case, but the witness is not a lawyer and, therefore, sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if we can go back for a moment to the April 7, 1992 article that you wrote, do you recall if you, in that article, gave any opinions or comments relating to whether or not the issues from the camps, Omarska and Trnopolje specifically, were not systematic and were not widespread?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I just ask you to say which article it was? You gave me a date and I'm not sure which one you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many articles did you write on August 7, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Belgrade immediately upon interviewing individuals in the Omarska and Trnopolje camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if I can interrupt you. I was asked by the interpreters to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recall whether or not in your article of August 7, 1992, whether you gave an opinion or impression that in fact there was not a systematic pattern and there was no widespread attack relating to the Prijedor area or region, namely from April through September 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'd read the article more recently, I would be of more assistance, but to the best of my recollection, I think the article gave a sense of destruction in the area. If you can produce it. I certainly wanted to try and reflect that there was tragic movement of refugees on both sides. But I think that we can go -- I can't remember that article, by think there's no doubt that my -- that that article and those that appeared in the very few weeks after it would have given the impression of a widespread - to use your term and not mine - a widespread and systematic persecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it not take much time before the Defence prepares or provides us with this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. If it could be distributed in order to enable the parties and the Judges to read this article during the break and immediately after the distribution by the usher we will have the break, but please, first distribute. Thank you. I think we should, in principle, proceed this way in order to facilitate the work, indeed it's the work of the witness, as it was done in the examination-in-chief. We have this document now available, but it's necessary to have a break now, and we will continue at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can I may one request? I think it would be fair to let the witness to have a copy of the article to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would like to be heard on that if I may, Your Honour. This witness has testified under oath about some amazingly specific recollections that he claims that he has. He gives us the background as having won the British Pulitzer Prize relating to this activities and his activities on August 5, 1992. This witness should tell us if he can't recall the items that he states in his article and then we'll do and proceed one of two ways which I think has been widely accepted here. One, we can impeach him on it if he tells us different, or two, we would refresh his recollection on items that he claims he does not recall at this time. His testimony yesterday, Your Honour, without summarising it, is being called in question specifically. This article he wrote we hope will clarify those points, but I think it would be unfair for the cross, unfair for the Defence, to have this witness now become what we would coin educated on his very own work. Either he has a recollection or he doesn't. If he does, we'd like to inquire about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness had the opportunity to discuss these issues and he told us, no doubt, it's extremely difficult for all of us to recollect issues in 1992, and it's only fair after you have, as you did already, tried out whether or not Mr. Vulliamy is able, to the best his recollection, to tell us what he wrote in this article to present now this document. We did this earlier, and I think it's balancing the interests of the parties. The OTP proceeded this way, and I think the Defence should do it in the same way. But nevertheless, it's mandatory to have the break now until 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, having had the opportunity to review the article during the break --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't actually, but I've got it in front of me and I'll certainly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a lot that you wrote in this article of August 7, 1992. I'm going to only just highlight so I can complete this one area relating to widespread and systematic patterns and just so that I can obtain from you what is it that you mean in the article. The article we'll hopefully come back to at a later time when we discuss issues of who was or was not in control of the meeting that you attended on April 5, 1992, what it is that you observed and learned during your visits to both Omarska and Trnopolje on October 5, 1992. But for our purposes now, I'm going to direct your attention specifically, if I may, to the third page of the article which on the top right-hand corner it says page 3 of 7.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last paragraph on that page. Second sentence in that last paragraph, it states: "And although there was no visible evidence of serious violence, let alone systematic extermination, inside the aluminum shed is something it was worth them breaking Dr. Karadzic's promise to avoid exposing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is your article, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the word "systematic," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that we didn't see any systematic extermination, by which I mean mass killing of individuals, that day in the camp before our eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you before your eyes also, sir, note that there was no visible evidence of serious violence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our very brief and restricted visit to Omarska that day, as I think I've already said and it's on the television, we did not get to see ourselves any -- well, I mentioned the wound, but I wouldn't call that systematic extermination. I didn't see any systematic extermination and that's what I'm saying here, but I think I go on to qualify that we had our suspicions about what was going on in the hut that they refused to allows us into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to the issue of "widespread," since the two seem at time to go hand-in-hand. If you could turn to page 6 of 7 of your same article, specifically paragraph 2 within that article. Yesterday, you were kind enough to share with the OTP your view of various homes that were either shelled or burned, as you claimed. Within this paragraph, sir, and just tell me if it's correct, you write: "But down the road are other Muslim villages intact, peasants calmly bringing in the hay." You didn't tell us yesterday that during your trip from Pale through Banja Luka to Prijedor that you saw Muslim villages that were intact; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a reference to the houses that I think I did mention outside which they were hanging white sheets or flags which, if it wasn't explained to us then, I now know to mean that they were awaiting deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that there were more, as you state in your article, not only homes but villages during your route that were completely intact prior to your arriving to Prijedor on August 5, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, if I can help best by going sort of town by town as I best recall. In Bijeljina, which is quite a large place, mostly -- the house were mostly intact that we saw. In a place called Brcko, the bit of town that we went through at least was very -- for the most part destroyed. And a place called Derventa, I recall there was some damage but not complete. And of course Kozarac I've already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this: In Trnopolje, sir, when you visited it, is it true that there were women and children there as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Trnopolje camp, yes. Yes. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, your article references that there were women and children there; correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same page, page 4 of 7?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the way, I didn't get this article during the break, so if you'll forgive me for taking counsel's cue and finding bits that he refers to. But there were women and children in Trnopolje, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recall interviewing both women, children, and men to determine that there was no violence, as you state at the bottom of page 4 of 7, the last paragraph that "'there was no violence against us, just hot and smelly,' adds her husband."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what one person said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write in your article that you don't believe the person that said that?
