utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- not -- I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also, on a different section in your article here, page 2 of 7, reference a gentleman by the name of Elezovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that gentleman at any time indicate to you whether there was any violence or harm done to him as a result of his detention in the Omarska or Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says it himself. "Personally, nobody touched me." But I certainly don't think that this man was in very good physical condition in terms of his weight and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, in fact --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's what he said, and that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recall that ten years later, that he was not in good condition. But in your article, on the fourth -- sixth paragraph, you state your own impression, your own observation, you state: "He shows no signs of beatings." Do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Let me just have a look. Yes, it's there. And he --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I wrote it, this man did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: When you gave the interviews which gave you some acclaim, if I may say so, and was the basis or foundation, if you will, of some of the awards that you received subsequent to that, did you include any of that in the interviews you gave where the public speeches you were giving related to Omarska and Trnopolje in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quote this man, as I recall, neither by name nor by quotation. By the time I was talking publicly in the way that you describe, I had quite quickly found out quite a lot more about Omarska and what was going on in Omarska from people who had walked the road that I described yesterday, and certainly -- well, this man has -- shows no signs of beating nor did he, nor did some -- or most of those in the canteen. But I was certainly not prepared to say in public that Omarska was a place, given what I subsequently learnt, in which people are left alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I -- may I just ask again you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time call Penny Marshall who was giving interviews for ITN or other newscasters to tell them that, in fact, apart from the undernourishment and the humiliation of the drill of the individuals that you saw at Omarska camp on August 5th, 1992, none of the 80 inmates, as you call them, showed signs of violence or beating?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any particular details of conversations with Penny Marshall, and I -- if I understand your question, I don't think, as I know, I don't -- as I recall, I don't think that we would have gone over the fact that none of the people we saw showed signs of beating because, as I've said and as you've said, they didn't. As regards public comments made since that time, I have researched Omarska more than I was able to do certainly that day, and have found it a place in which many people were very seriously abused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just interested to know what your impressions were on August 5, 1992. And since we have to article that you wrote two days later, essentially contemporaneous, if you will, with the events that transpired on that day, you write on page 2 of that same article that very conclusion, that based upon your observation and your impressions, you could not see and were unable to determine whether any of the inmates, in fact, were abused, beaten, or in any way violently treated; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've seen yesterday that we -- that our access to the camp was extremely limited and restricted, and we were shown the canteen area only. We were then taken upstairs to an office complex, treated to a long briefing, and then when we tried to get into other parts of the camp, we were basically bundled out. And it's true that none of the people we saw or, rather, we were shown showed any signs of beating, apart from one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your visit, if you will, to the Trnopolje camp was obviously less restrictive; correct? You were able to walk around. And in fact there was one detainee who took you off to the side and showed you the interior of one of the buildings within the Trnopolje complex or compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were able to formulate at that time your impressions of the Trnopolje camp, were you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, not unlimited, but I formulated an impression of the Trnopolje camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not, sir, write in this article on August 7thg, 1992, formulate your opinion and impression that in fact Trnopolje camp was not a "concentration camp"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how much the Court wants to get into the semantics of the word "concentration camp." I, at the time, did not want to use the word, and I've written this before, because the next day connections were being made and the connotations of that word, I thought, were being misused. In subsequently talking about it, I have gone back over the history of the term, dating back principally to South Africa at the beginning of this century, and have come to the conclusion that given that it was a place where people were collected for enforced deportation, that it was not a bad -- it is a usable term, if not the term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, don't you conclude, sir, that the very use of the word "concentration" by way of definition is a collection of people within a specific area and that the use of the term "concentration camp" is not in any way related to what history has shown us from World War II, namely Auschwitz, among other such camps; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we're to talk about the history of the word. The reason I was reticent to use the word at the time with regard to Trnopolje is because I think that in recent history or at least in the last half century, the word has come to mean, wrongly, synonymous with a death camp or an extermination camp. I, in trying to choose my words carefully, went back over the history of the term "concentration camp" which does accord exactly with your definition as first used by the British in South Africa during the Boer war, a rounding up and collection or enforced collection of people prior -- well, in at that case for permanent internment or prior to this enforced deportation in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You use the word "deportation." Do you have a definition for me of that word?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My definition of deportation would be what I described yesterday from my first-hand experience, of people being herded in a convoy from their homes over the mountains at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your trip that you claim you took on August 17, 1992, up to and through Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my firsthand experience. I've obviously spoken to large numbers of people who have different experiences who were deported from the Prijedor area and other areas in Bosnia, Eastern Bosnia and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just so I can understand --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And other areas of former Yugoslavia, not just Croatians and Muslims but indeed Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to all that in a minute, but just for my limited purpose so I can fully understand your definition of "deportation," your trip that you claim you took on August 17, 1992, it was a voluntary trip that you made. You actually joined the convoy; correct? You snuck in, joined it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trip that I claimed I made and did make on August the 17th was in the case of myself and my colleagues voluntary but it was not voluntary in the case of the several hundred other people on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as your definition for "deportation," would it have that you were being deported?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't being deported. I was trying to report deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One was a voluntary act by you and your colleague and the others, you're presuming, was an involuntary act; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was a professional inquiry, voluntary professional inquiry, if that's the right term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've never heard the term, but I'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the execution of my profession to inquire into what seemed to be going on in the area and I inferred or, rather, it was made pretty clear from everybody we spoke to during that day and night that so far as they were concerned, their -- the deportation was extremely involuntary. It was enforced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with me this: How many people did you interview who were accompanying you with -- on this convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, but during the day and night -- well, during the day obviously fewer people because we were in cars, but we were walking for several hours and would have spoken to, I don't know, 20, 25 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of how many people, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought about 1.600 on the convoy altogether. Then we joined then too when they were looking for parts of -- for space on the floors of gymnasia or schools in Travnik which were already packed full of people who had come the same way, and many were to follow. We spent time during the night interviewing others who had been on the convoy as well. So I'm saying 20, 25, 30. We were chatting during the night with large numbers of people, exchanging their recollections of what had happened to them over the last 24, 48 hours. And their marshalling into the convoy and the reasons why they had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just going back to the Trnopolje camp, and I apologise if we took a little detour here on this but we'll come back to the issue of what you call deportation a little later today. You, in fact, sir, immediately following your visit on the August 5th, 1992, at the Trnopolje camp made a qualitative opinion, if you will, opinion and impression as to how to describe this camp. In fact you state in your article of August 7, 1992 that the camp can be described as something between a civilian prison and a transit camp, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I can't -- as I say, I apologise to you and the Court. I haven't had a chance to read this during the break, but I'll take it from you, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but just so the record is clear, I'll direct your attention to it if I may. Page 4 of 7, the same paragraph where we were just discussing where you said Trnopolje cannot be called a "concentration camp," and immediately thereafter you identify it or quantify or qualify how it can be described. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you help me by telling me which paragraph is it, sir? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fifth paragraph on that page. We were just discussing it ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As regards the first sentence, I hope I've covered that. We can go back over it if you'd like. But this was written on a day when I was giving interviews by people who were, I thought, trying to equate the word "concentration camp" with "extermination camp" or "death camp." There was a headline that I particularly thought illustrated this, and it was rather silly, which said "Belsen 92" in one newspaper. That's clearly not what it was so that's why I'm illustrating that. Well, the civilian prison would refer to the fenced-off area in which the prisoners that we saw yesterday on the video, who'd come from Omarska and Trnopolje were being confined in an area, and transit camp would refer to other bits of the camp, some of which we also saw on the video yesterday, to which people had come for a number of reasons, either in flight from attacks on their homes or marshalled in columns and frog marched there, awaiting deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what other areas did you note these transit camps throughout your experience in 1991 through 1996 in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned the camp run by the Croatians near the town of Capljina, and I went there twice, and of course Keraterm is mentioned here. I read reports of other camps, but I didn't visit any myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier today when I started the cross-examination, I asked you about embellishing and distorting facts as a reporter and your obligations to report only the facts and the facts as you saw them. Help me with this if you don't mind, Mr. Vulliamy: Your article, two days later, would you agree with me that it is actually a reliable and trustworthy source depicting what those impressions were that you had and observations that were made on or about August 5, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the best I could do based on my impressions of that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anything subsequent to that such as your testimony in the Tadic case or your testimony in the Blaskic case or your testimony in the Kovacevic case or your testimony in the Sikirica case would all, having come subsequent to this, those are all things that if they're not within this report would be items that you learned from other sources or, as I've identified, being embellishment of the truth or the facts as they truly existed on or about August 5, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- you're talking about embellishments and distortions. I learned an awful lot about Trnopolje and Omarska after writing -- subsequent to writing this article, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But our focus is here, if I may, with all due respect, is to obtain what your impressions were as of August 5th. Not what you later learned, whether through your discussions with the OTP or books you may have read or other sources that you may have consulted. We're interested to know what the parties did at that given time. Would you agree with me that it is this article and this source which is the most reliable and most trustworthy since it was made contemporaneous, if you will, as you state, with the events that took place less than two days prior?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The sources, by the way, that I consulted with were not books and -- so much -- or Prosecutor so much as people who had been in the camps or their relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do know that you interviewed some of these people that were in the camps, but I dare say that in this article where you interviewed two such individuals, specifically Mr. Elezovic and the other individual, you have never mentioned either this conversation with those individuals in any of the five trials that you've given testimony in, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I'm afraid. But if you -- you perhaps reviewed the material more closely than I have. But I can't remember what you -- you asked me two questions at once. I can't remember what the first one was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpreters to catch up, sir. With respect -- are we ready?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in this article you identified individuals that at the time you were left with the impression who had responsibility or control, if you will, for access to the Omarska and Trnopolje camp, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may answer your question previously, which I didn't answer. Frankly, I -- in remarks I've made subsequently about Omarska and Trnopolje, my belief that we were given pretty short shrift in Omarska has been confirmed, as is the belief that we were shown an unrepresentative group of prisoners. And if I have not mentioned Mr. Elezovic since then, I expect it's because I didn't think that his -- that his remarks were particularly representative of what I subsequently learned was going on in Omarska and which was hidden from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can take you to your journey on -- towards the end of July 1992 up until August 5, 1992, you arrived in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also shared with us that immediately prior to that, you were also in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, very briefly. Oh, and, sorry, on -- we were taken to the Serbian side of Sarajevo from Pale to around the hills above the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the time frame of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This was the -- we went from Belgrade to Pale by helicopter on the morning of -- I'm trying to work backwards from the 5th, which is the day, of course, I remember. On the morning of the 3rd. So we would have gone to Sarajevo and the Serbian side and visited the Kula prison and some positions above the city and a military hospital on that afternoon into early evening on the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your visit to Kula was actually before your visit to Omarska and Trnopolje? I understood your testimony yesterday to be slightly different. I'm trying to locate the page number of that. It was my understanding, correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Vulliamy, that it was after the visit to Omarska and Trnopolje, at the insistence of Serbs such as Professor Koljevic, you decided to check to see whether there was any truth or substance to their claim that Serbs were held in detention centres or camps by the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry if there's some confusion. Can I help to clarify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- please. I'm sure you can.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I can quite easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question. It might work a little bit better. August 5th we know you're in Omarska and Trnopolje. Prior to that you're in Belgrade approximately July 28 to the 29. We understand your testimony that you took a helicopter from Belgrade to Pale and then ultimately through Banja Luka and arrived at Prijedor municipality. My question to you: Prior to those events, is it true that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to when? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to July 28, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went very briefly into the airport. On the siege, the developing siege of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you weren't reporting on any Serb refugees or Serbs who were inmates or prisoners of Muslim detention centres, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I can just get back to this order of things with reference to your previous question. I notice that you've got us here in Belgrade from the 2nd of July to the 29th, but it wasn't that long. I think it was from the 29th to August the 3rd, visiting some of the other places like Loznica that I went into yesterday. We travelled from, as you said, Belgrade to Pale on the 3rd and went to Kula, which I think it was called Kula, that night, which is where Serbs were holding Muslims in a place that didn't, frankly, concern me very much, relatively speaking. And then it was after going to Omarska and Trnopolje that I thought it was appropriate to -- to -- well, accept and investigate Vice-President Koljevic's allegations about the camps in which the Serbs were being held. And the advice was that the worst of those was at a place called Capljina, and that's the one I went to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where that was? Was that a camp that was held by Croatians or a camp that was held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held by a militia called the HOS, and it was in Herzegovina, in the south of the country, and the make-up of the HOS was mixed, actually. It was a Croatian -- I mean, it went under a Croatian, if you like, sort of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vernacular?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And certainly a Croatian heraldry, but there were a number of Muslims in the HOS for political reasons that I can explain if you like, but it was a mixed militia but under a Croatian, as you say, vernacular or heraldry. And the conditions there, as I said yesterday, were bad. We ran quite a major story on it, pages 1 and 3, entitled "Secrets of the Croat camp."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question though is did you at any time, sir, subsequent to August 5, 1992, did you ever visit any camps that existed that the Muslims were holding Serbian citizens or Serbian inmates?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to any other camps after that apart from a second visit to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then I don't understand your testimony when you say on August 7th, after you met with Vice-President Koljevic you wanted to take him up on his offer. Isn't it true that the Serbs at that time were asking that the international press and foreign journalists such as yourself investigate Muslim controlled detention centres and/or camps to determine how many Serbs may be inmates or prisoners within those camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if that was the exact wording. I did try to find a camp where Muslims were holding Serbs in a tunnel, and I'm afraid I can't remember the name of the place but with a map I could. I think it was Tarcin or something. A railway tunnel or a road tunnel. But there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to verify any of this, did you make an attempt to go to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the Celebici camp at or about that time where vice-president, Professor Koljevic, would have identified that as one of the camps which at that time held Serbian citizens in a Muslim detention centre?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware of Celebici now. If it was on the list, then I would have read the name, but I don't recall reading the name. The ones that were emphasised were Capljina and, as I say, this railway tunnel, and I think the railway tunnel or the road tunnel was called Tarcin, but I would like to check that with a map to get the name or the spelling right. But I did go there to the tunnel, but there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also did not, at any time prior or subsequent to April 5th, 1992, visit any detention centres operated and controlled by the Muslims holding Serbian citizens in the area of Bihac, did you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Bosnia before April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I always say April. I meant August. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't really in Bosnia before August. I mean, I was there in Sarajevo airport for about 36 hours. The events that we described yesterday was the first real reporting I did in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just help me understand, then. What is it you did after vice-president Professor Koljevic wanted you to go out and verify whether Serbs were held in Muslim detention centres? Was it nothing? Was it very, very limited, or did you actually go out and investigate these camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is it that I did? I went and did it. I didn't join what I called the media circus going down to Trnopolje and Omarska, and I drove through Hungary or through the day and the best part after night down onto the other side. And the one they seemed most concerned about was this one at Capljina and quite rightly so. The conditions were appalling, and I reported that. Was the access limited? It wasn't -- well, yes, it was. We were not allowed to go into and we were whisked past the hangar where they were keeping the women, and that was -- I mean, apart from the general conditions, that was the nub of the story. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a foreign correspondent and journalist, when you were told in the Trnopolje camp of the existence of the Keraterm camp, did you report it anywhere and did you do anything to investigate the existence of that camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went to Belgrade as quickly as we could to file what we already had. And there were reports of a massacre in that camp which I heard about that day, but could not corroborate, could not prove, and quite honestly with an allegation of that size, one is not going to rush into print with it on the basis of one's -- you know, of one or two pieces of testimony. I mean, had he said five people, one might have done so. But, no. We felt that at the end of the August the 5th, and I think our hosts felt, at least they made us feel that it was time to go and to -- well, in our case, report what we'd found and in their case I think to get these people out of here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the opposite occurred. More people came; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by which time, I think, things had changed during the interim period. And I'm talking not from personal experience here, but I believe that from the reporting that I've read, fences had come down, a thing had gone up in English saying Trnopolje Reception Centre, and from the research I've done since that day, I gather that Omarska was if not closed, almost closed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a couple years after your visit to the Omarska and Trnopolje camps, you wrote a book; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote a book in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was published in 1994, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was completed before 1994. It was written in -- yeah, in five weeks, published early 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I understand how journalists operate, in fact, within that book you would have a far better memory of the events that transpired on August 5th, 1992, than you would, let's say, today, and you would have made such recordations within that book; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have a better memory because it's closer in time. I would have known more about the places I was writing about because I was writing it a year later and had talked to a lot of people, had been in -- in the area quite a bit. But when I -- or if I ever look at the book now, I know a lot more now than I do then -- than I did then. I mean, I have not left the subject completely alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in things such as identifying individuals who may have been in charge or in control or who may have been chairman of certain meetings that took place August 5th, 1992. Wouldn't you agree with me that within that book, having written it, several or a couple of years after the events, it would have a far more reliable source than your recollection sitting here today as to who may have been the person in charge or responsible of Omarska Detention Centre or Trnopolje camp, would they not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine they might probably be the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if they're not, which do you, sir, believe are more reliable and trustworthy, one having been written a year to two after the events or your recollection of the events ten years later?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in anticipation of your questions, I'll say the book is closer to the time, but I know more about the situation now than then. As regards the meeting of 1992, I'll say the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And similarly, the article that you wrote on August 7th, 1992, having been written only two days from the events which you're here testifying about, August 5th, 1992, that also would, wouldn't you agree, be more reliable and trustworthy as to who was the person that may have been in charge or in control of the detention centres than your testimony here ten years after the event?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should think so. The article in -- August 5, 1992, would have been without talking to Penny Marshall and Ian Williams. But it would be -- I don't know what -- we're talking about what I'm saying now, would it be more accurate than what I'm about to say? I don't know what I'm about to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified already about the August 5th, 1992 meeting as to who was in charge of that meeting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you testified about that on several other trials as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about it certainly once, in the trial of, sadly deceased Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not testify about it in the Tadic case where specifically you identified Dr. Stakic as being a person who "nominally" [Realtime transcript read in error "normally"] was involved in the events that occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the word "nominally," although it certainly makes sense. And I'm sure I was asked to recall the meeting, the 1992 meeting, in the Tadic trial. It wouldn't make sense if I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, if I may, to the Tadic transcript for the Court and the OTP. But just before I do that, I have a request, I think on line 8 there's a word that's placed in quotes, "normally," and I think it was my question and because I spoke a little too quick, the word should be "nominally". If I could reflect that for the record. And I think the witness incorporating the word in his answer was able to assist us a little bit.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nominally I've got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Direct you go -- directing your attention to the testimony in the Dusko Tadic case, which took place on or about June 6, 1996, specifically page 1460 [Realtime transcript read in error "1416"]. In describing the events relating to Dr. Stakic and those of August 5, 1992, you proceeded to testify that you wanted to go back to see the individuals so that you could interview some of the players that you had met four years later. So you're talking about the reasons why you went back in February of 1996.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. And I was -- I was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read it for you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On line 20 specifically, you state, page 1416: "So I thought would be interesting to go and find him again. I also wanted to find Mr. Stakic, the mayor, the rather bald-headed gentleman who was nominally in charge of the operation, so I set about looking for all three of them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I would be more than happy to follow. You're quoting the 7th of June, 1996, page 1416?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It appeared on line 22 as 1416.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me understand what you mean when you use the word "nominally."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was the man in charge. He was the number one. He was the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So "nominal" to you means he's number one; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the top official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this. During the Kovacevic trial do you remember your testimony that you were of the opinion that relating to the August 5th, 1992 meeting that Dr. Kovacevic was the chairman and the man in charge?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, but certainly Dr. Kovacevic was the man, as it were, in the middle of the table, and he was doing most of the talking. In charge is whether we're talking about numbers of words spoken during a meeting or rank, you could apply it to either or neither.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to understand, sir, who you felt was the individual who was in charge at the meeting or, as you have coined it previously in your testimony under oath in the Kovacevic case, the chairman of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I used the word chairman. If I did it would apply to both or neither in a way. One of the gentlemen has the top rank. The other did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and direct our attention to the page you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically page 780 and 781 of the Kovacevic transcript. I think it starts to overlap a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you state -- the question was asked, "during the meeting of August 5th, 1992, did you form an opinion" - this is a question to you, Mr. Vulliamy, four years ago - "did you form an opinion as to who was in charge of the meeting? Who was running the meeting?" Question answered by you as a somewhat respectfully I must say long-winded attempt, you conclude unequivocally that it was Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- I don't know if I said unequivocally, and I don't know what the long-winded, roundabout way is, but certainly he did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it now your testimony that the person who was in charge of the meeting and who was running the meeting was in fact Dr. Stakic and not Dr. Kovacevic or does it really make a difference depending upon where you testify, Mr. Vulliamy, and that your opinion changes by the day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. My testimony is that the late Dr. Kovacevic was certainly -- dominated the meeting. He did most of the talking. Questions and answers were directed at him. Mr. Stakic said much less. And my testimony is simply that they were the numbers one and two at that meeting. But I'm not going to change my view of who was making the most -- or making the most contribution to the meeting, nor am I going to change any view I've said or not said about how they were introduced in terms of rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'm not asking you to change it. I'm asking you simply to reconcile it for me. In 1998, on page 780 of your transcript, under oath, under the penalty of perjury, you were asked who was in charge of that meeting and who was running the meeting. You didn't say, "Oh, it was both Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic." You in fact said unequivocally that it was Dr. Kovacevic. How can you reconcile the two formulations? I think there's an objection, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, previously the Court has indicated that to be fair to a witness that an entire answer giving the context be read out. Counsel's really only discussed though he hasn't read out the very last two lines of an answer that he called long-winded but which is about ten lines. And I think it would be only fair to have read out the answer that the witness gave quite a few years ago to be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Especially with the fact that unfortunately we are not provided with this special testimony. So it also assists our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, on page 780 of the Kovacevic trial, on July 15, 1998, you were asked by your friend Mr. Keegan, on line 19: "Q. Mr. Vulliamy, during this meeting, did you form an opinion as to who was in charge of the meeting, who was running the meeting?" Answer, which commences on line 22 of page 708 is always follows: "A. Well, thus far the man doing most of the talking up until this point was, if you like, the chairman of the meeting, or at least he was the one who was making the most pertinent remarks, and I found them interesting remarks because even before we had asked the question, we were talking about concentration camps and now he was defining what we were about to see as not concentration camps but transit camps and talking about British intelligence's failure to identify the Nazi camps in the '40s. I thought we were in the domain." You proceed to say "Sorry to answer your question, 'Mr. Kovacevic' is the answer." You yourself put quotes while giving that answer to Mr. Keegan four years ago that you were unequivocal that you even put quotes on it and said that there was no doubt in answering Mr. Keegan's question as to whether or not you formed an opinion as to who the person was who was in charge of the meeting you found it was Dr. Kovacevic, as you called him Mr. Kovacevic at that time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say unequivocally as you said I said, and my -- and you called Mr. Keegan a friend. I don't have a social relationship with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He definitely knows --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, no. Everybody knows, and you wrote about it, didn't you that in fact you even borrowed one of his suits to testify, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't write about that in any article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I needed to borrow a suit to testify because I was brought in court hurriedly and I was in a pair of jeans at the time and the witness order changed. And I borrowed a suit off somebody else actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, anyway, call him whatever you want, your friend or not. I didn't think it was an offensive comment to --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It might give an impression that I think is -- does not describe the situation, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, help me with this. Reconcile it for me. Who was in charge on August 5th, 1992 of that meeting in which you attended and of which we saw a seven-minute clip of?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I'll go -- stand by what I said. We saw on the tape Dr. Kovacevic open the remarks on the film, talk at great length, and we -- I don't know whether it was on the film, but I was interested in all this stuff about concentration camps in the 1940s. He was the man in the middle of the table and he was doing most of the talking. He dominated the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this. I'm going to try to ask this question. I have to read it: What part of the meeting gave you the impression beyond the fact that he was giving you introductory remarks that he, Dr. Kovacevic, was in control of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the meeting. I mean, as I've said, he talked more than anybody else throughout the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me compare it to what you said when Mr. Keegan asked you that question during Dr. Kovacevic's trial. That very same question was asked on page 781. Again 781, line 10: "What part of the meeting gave you the impression beyond the fact that he was giving you introductory remarks that he was in control of the meeting?" Your response --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can remember the gesture, if that's what you're going to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to it. We have your answer and we'll get to it. Your answer which starts on line 14 of that same page: "In control of the talking, certainly, yes. I got the impression that he was the man who was opening the proceedings and chairing the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he exercise the -- did you note him? For example, on the film exercising control over the conduct of the other participants answer line 20.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a moment where his boss, Mayor Stakic tries to make a contribution and he, Dr. Kovacevic, shuts him up. Yes, he was delivering this monologue and --" And then you were interrupted by Mr. Keegan at that time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember the gesture when I think Mr. -- Mr. Kovacevic is talking, and I don't remember this that well, but to the best of my recollection and this is, I think, has been shown on a video, so any recollections are coloured by the video which I have seen since and will remember better, as I think -- I think Kovacevic is talking, and I think Stakic tries to come in and he waves his hand and Mr. Stakic stops talking. Yeah, he does shut him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That at least in 1998 gave you a factor in formulating your impression that there was no doubt Dr. Kovacevic was the man in charge; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I have used the words "in charge." You have, and I think it's somewhere in the questions from the previous trial, I just keep coming back to this: Yes, he opened the meeting. He was sitting at the table. He was, if you like -- I'll say if you set out the table he was in -- the chairman of the board sits in the middle, then he was sitting in the middle. Well, not quite in the middle because there were four of them, and Mr. Stakic was out on the edge. And I'll stand by this, yes. He was the dominant voice in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was more than dominant n fact, in your answer you say he was in control of the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would take them to be if not synonymous, in fact pretty close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you go on to say he was chairman of the meeting, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it again today. There are four people along the thing. He's one of the two in the middle. He makes the initial -- sort of, after the argument that I described with Colonel Arsic, he makes the first sort of welcoming or -- actually, it was unwelcoming remarks before Mr. Stakic makes his contribution. He speaks first and he speaks most. Mr. Stakic is his boss. That's really all I can help you with on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. And two days after this when you wrote are article on August 7, 1992, you again only identified Dr. Kovacevic as the person who was president of the executive council of Prijedor and is "technically responsible for Omarska and Trnopolje," do you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 6 of 7, 7th paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please for the transcript read out the entire paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "Firstly, that of Milan Kovacevic who as president of the executive council of Prijedor is technically responsible for Omarska and Trnopolje. He was born in Jasenovac, the Croatian Ustasha camp, where 750 Serbs and Jews were killed between 1941 and 1945."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I concede to having made a mistake, because Mr. Kovacevic is not -- was not the president of the executive council of Prijedor, and I don't have my shorthand notes in front of me, but to the best of my recollection, it says "Stakic prez" and then by Kovacevic's name it says "vice-president". But I -- well, I -- you can tell me better if I've got this wrong, but I was given to understand that Mr. Kovacevic was actually the vice-president, and I don't know why it doesn't say that here. I don't think that would have been my error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that, but even after that, you state that Dr. Kovacevic was born in the Jasenovac camp, and in fact you subsequently learned, did you not, sir, that that is inaccurate? In fact, your notes that you read to us yesterday from the February 1996 meeting clearly clarify for us that you're wrong on that point as well; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not born in Jasenovac but only did spend some time there as a minor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which is the truth, actually, because I know and noted that he told us on August the 5th that he had been born in that awful place. And when I went back to see him for the second time, he said that he'd spent some time there as a boy. I don't know which is the exact -- which version is the correct one, but whichever, I found it to be an interesting and indeed moving detail in this article, as you see I call it the Serbian counterargument to the accusations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever, sir, when you find or learn that, in fact, facts that you wrote in an article or inaccurate or incorrect, do you ever prepare and publish a follow-up article or a subsequent article and identify where those errors may or may not have appeared?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- obviously if there'd been some communication from Mr. Kovacevic to correct this citing of him or in fact indeed any subsequent citing of him, if there are any contacts or corrections made, for instance, if he had written and said "no, well, I wasn't actually born in Jasenovac, but I was taken there as a boy by my aunt," as I later heard then of course we'd publish some kind of correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever sent the article to him in a language which he could understand or did you presume he spoke and can read English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how would you expect him, then, to go ahead and respond to the article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question, including two issues we have only one no. The no is true that you didn't send the article to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not practice to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I can clarify if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's true, Mr. Vulliamy, you did not send Dr. Kovacevic a copy of the August 7th, 1992 article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a journalist, as a reporter investigating things such as camps and identifying individuals who, as you put it, are "technically responsible" for certain camps, didn't you yourself have an obligation ethically to determine and confirm that the facts upon which you've printed are reliable and trustworthy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is a very circular question, not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this, sir, in the meeting that was taking place on August 5th, 1992, how many people participated or were in that room?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's hard to say. Your Honour, I'll have to reflect a bit. There were, for a start, a number of people coming in and out of the room at different points of this long meeting, leaning against the radiator. In particular I remember -- or coming in and out, checking it out, checking the situation out. Some in uniform, some not. But I'm sorry the participants, the principal participants we'll say Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic, Colonel Arsic, Mr. Drljaca, Mrs. Balaban, the interpreter for ITN, myself, Penny Marshall, Ian Williams, the Bosnian Serb television crew, cameramen and soundmen from ITN, the ITN producer, PA woman. I think somebody else was taking photographs or a film, but I don't know who that might have been. That's -- those are the main participants, and I'm sorry to be long-winded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's about 20, 25 people? Is that your estimate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many that is who I've listed, but if we add a few unknown and unnamed to me less than 20. More like 12 to 15 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. 12 to 15. Now, you had obtained authorisation or at least ITN did to be able to visit Omarska prior to August 5th, 1992, as you described to us yesterday, and then you proceeded to go to Belgrade in order to obtain what kind of documentation so that you could have access to the region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: ITN and myself were given --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yourself, yes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Were given a guarantee that we would go to Omarska. We arrived in Belgrade and we got accreditation from the -- the -- the Bosnian Serb press agency had an office in Belgrade. Srna rings a bell, but I'm not certain that that was it and we had to go to their office or a desk in other office, I'm not sure which, and get accreditation there. And I think we probably would have had some sort of accreditation from the federal authorities as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was this written accreditation that you obtained?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sort of stamped bit of paper as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retain a copy of those papers that would have accredited you and ITN to be able to go and visit Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would have shown it to authorities at various checkpoints. I don't have it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this: Who decided that you should meet with the local representatives of the Prijedor municipality prior to being taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You identified yesterday in your testimony that you were told that you were going to meet individuals and what you identify as being "a Crisis Committee." The Court asked you a follow-up question on that. My question to you with respect to that issue is: Who is the individual who identified these members that you were about to visit as being "Crisis Committee" members?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I this was it the police chief Mr. Drljaca when we were coming up the stairs first used the term. I will concede that it could have been Crisis Staff or Crisis Committee. I really can't remember which it was, but it was crisis whatever. And I think the term was first used by Mr. Drljaca. In answer to your previous question, I should say I don't know who decided that we should meet with them, but it seemed that we were being passed down a chain of command. Karadzic, Koljevic, and it was logical that this was the sort of next step. And of course Major Milutinovic from Banja Luka knew where we were going, but I don't know if he had decided that that's where we were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know if in the contemporaneous notes that you kept relating to the August 5, 1992 meeting or anywhere in the video captions that we've seen of the meeting on August 5, 1992, whether at any time any individual identifies this group of men as being members of a "Crisis Committee"? Does it appear in your notes anywhere?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it appear anywhere on the video that you reviewed prior to testifying and including those videos that you viewed yesterday in open court?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what -- I don't know if it's on the video. We would have been introduced at a time when I -- you know, the notebook probably wasn't even open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite frankly, Mr. Vulliamy, I did read your prior testimony, and I'm hard pressed to find anywhere within that testimony that the deceased, Simo Drljaca, or any individual has identified you, identified those people as being members of a "Crisis Committee." My question to you is: Are you telling us 10 years later that you have a specific and vivid recollection of the late Simo Drljaca telling you that this was a "Crisis Committee"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you what I've already said. One is that I think it was him on the way up the stairs who first used the term, and it's not that vivid because I can't remember whether it was "Crisis Committee" or - that was my recollection - and then when His Honour said was it "Crisis Staff," that also rang a bell, and I testified that I leave it open that it could be either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you did a lot of research subsequent to the events of August 5, 1992. Do you know whether or not on or about August 5, 1992, in fact there was not an existence of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that surprising because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't like to use that word "surprising" here. I'm just kidding. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I find that surprising because that's a word using -- that something -- crisis something was used to us that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Tadic case, in the Blaskic case, in the Kovacevic case, in the Sikirica Keraterm case, you've never shared the view that Simo Drljaca identified these people during this meeting as being members of a "Crisis Committee."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Unless he was asked that and the counsel can point to the question and the answer or lack of one, I don't think it's fair to ask the witness to be volunteered information that was not asked of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You testified on those four prior occasions. During your testimony on those cases as we've highlighted, for example, in the Dusko Tadic case you spoke specifically about the August 5, 1992 meeting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you tried to share with the Court in an open and honest manner all the details that you had relating to that meeting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, I looked through that testimony, and your recollection is probably far stronger than mine, but do you remember at any time sharing with the Court under oath that Simo Drljaca identified the members you were about to meet as being those from a "Crisis Committee"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, and I don't recall being asked what they were called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this if you can: Yesterday you testified about Colonel Arsic making a gesture with his hand and saying if you wished to go to the camp Omarska, talk to these individuals, and he gestured or you said he raised his hand. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, it was your conclusion at that time that the people who would be able to give you access to the camps were the two gentleman to the right of Colonel Arsic, namely Dr. Kovacevic and next to him Dr. Stakic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He implied all three of the other men, though, including Mr. Drljaca. The civilian authorities basically, not the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't imply it. Didn't he actually say it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if he actually said it, but he said not the military authorities. Manjaca, he made it clear to us, was under the command of the military authorities, and it was his authority -- under his authority that we could go to Manjaca, and if we wanted to go to Omarska, we would need the authority of the civilian authorities. And he said this would be all -- well, I mean he -- the three representatives of the civilian authorities in the room, Stakic, Kovacevic, Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that meeting, there was no discussion about Trnopolje, was there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from me. I think I heard Penny Marshall on the video mention it. So although I -- I mean, the video colours the recollection, unfortunately. I would say yes, there was. I heard it on the film yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify as to whether or not Colonel Arsic had quoted Simo Drljaca as the man in charge. On page 785 of your July 15, 1998 transcript discussing again the gesture -- I don't know if I should read the entire thing but I guess I will. Question line 13:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your question and answer segment with Colonel Arsic, how did it end, his participation? Answer line 15:

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a while, Colonel Arsic up on his Manjaca idea. He shrugged and said, "Well, I can't give permission to go to Omarska. If you want to go to Omarska" - and Trnopolje was also being mentioned but Omarska mainly - he gestured to his right and said, "you need to talk to these men because they're in charge of Omarska and Trnopolje." Line 22:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was on his right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic. And then, Mr. Vulliamy, you proceed to add: "He also said that we would need to speak to Mr. Drljaca but his gesture was in this direction." Do you remember giving that testimony approximately four years ago?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it, but it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you in fact, sir, or any members of the team -- I'm going a little too fast. Did you in fact, sir, or any members of the ITN team who were in Prijedor on August 5, 1992, ask or talk to Simo Drljaca about gaining access to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca took us to the camp. He was there, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw him on the video, but did you ask him for permission to go to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were asking all -- everybody in the room for permission to go to the camp at various points in the meeting. I mean all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were asked by the OTP who in fact could have given you this access to the camp, you restricted your answer only to Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I mean -- well, I'll add -- I mean, we were asking them as a group of people fairly continuously over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just quickly because we only have a couple of minutes left, Just quickly in your book, I noted a couple interesting issues, and if I could cover one. Within your book that you wrote in 1993 and published in 1994, page 8 of that book, first full paragraph, you identify Milan Kovacevic, and you identify him as being the man responsible for the delivery of Muslim prisoners to the Omarska concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a fair -- that's a fair inference of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not inferring anything. I'm reading it directly from your book.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: Do not mention and do not identify Dr. Milomir Stakic as being the individual who is responsible for the delivery of prisoners to Omarska camp. You, in fact, only identify one person, and that person being the late Milan Kovacevic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a section that opens, as I recall - I haven't seen it for a while - that's a section that opens with a part of that meeting in which we're being shown various maps by Mr. Kovacevic, and indeed that's -- that's -- that's a quote from the book, and it's -- and it's -- I think it's true. I think Mr. Stakic appears elsewhere in the book if not somewhere during the opening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 100 you do identify Dr. Stakic, and you identify him as being the "civilian" mayor, And then you proceed to identify again his deputy Milan Kovacevic, and then you proceed to say what Milan Kovacevic's job was as follows: "Whose job it is to oversee the transit centres, including Omarska, and who was himself born in Jasenovac in 1941." Also on that page, 92 pages later, you again identify only Dr Kovacevic as being the person who oversees the camps and the person who is responsible for the camps, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it, but if you say so, yes, because Dr. Kovacevic was responsible for the camps as the deputy to Dr. Stakic. He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At no time in your book or in your article of August 7, 1992, do you identify Dr. Stakic as being the person who is either in control or responsible for any of the activities involving the people who were detained in either Omarska or Trnopolje; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it is. He said much less and he is what I said he was, the civilian mayor, the top official.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's the appropriate time, but in order that we don't lose control on the exhibits, I take it that the Defence tenders this article, "The Guardian," dated Friday, August 7, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would then go as DPD1, deposition taking Defence 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What -- sorry. What about the book? Is it your intention to tender the book as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's copyright laws that I just want to make sure I don't violate in terms of photocopying a text, a book, that the author is here unless and he could waive that. But in all seriousness, I think based on his testimony, it's unnecessary to have the entire book. We do have two extra copies that we took the liberty of preparing and photocopying, but it's at the Court's pleasure. Or the OTP, I'm sure, if they have the book can produce it. I'll make whatever accommodations the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I recollect copyright correctly, it allows for making copies of, depending on the country, 20 to 25 copies. So this shouldn't be any obstacle. But we are more than happy to receive copies of the parts, of the relevant parts, of this book and they may then go under DPD2. There was a comment by the OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't believe we've marked the video that was played today, which had not been played before. It was an excerpt from a video with the ERN number V000-0662, beginning at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be the next DP number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be DP7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: DP7. Thank you. Let's have the break now until thirty minutes past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence may continue immediately, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never like to give cautionary remarks to a witness, but I do that for two reasons if I may be permitted, and that is one, to remind myself of the rule that I would hope that you also follow, sir, and that is since we both speak English, we're overlapping a bit, and it's truly my fault more than yours, so don't take any of the comments as being negative. If you can just wait until I finish the question or reasonably when you think I've finished the question, and I'll try to do the same after you've completed your answer. Our translators are having some difficulty following me and then you as well. So can we agree on that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Court has also asked the same thing, and I apologise about any problems so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm troubled personally about a couple of things, and I'll get back to this issue of control, I do have a number of issues related to that, but on the question of the word "nominal," I had some time during the break to actually look up the word in a thesaurus, and you being an English journalist, the thesaurus that I looked at, which using the English language, states that the meaning of the word "nominal" is supposed, small, so-called, in name only, and inconsequential. Do you agree that the meaning of the word "nominal" is that which I've just described or do you continue to insist that it means top official, as you identified and told us, immediately before the break?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take the word to mean and used it to mean titular as in title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You disagree with the other comment as I call them, definitions and meanings of the word nominal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. First of all, the thesaurus does not give definitions, but synonyms and secondly, whether he agrees or disagrees with the synonyms of various meaning or shades of meaning in a thesaurus is not relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained. Maybe we can use four different thesauruses - it's a difficult word - but it's not important what this book tells us but what the intention of the witness before us was, what he wanted to express by his own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to ask you this question, Mr. Vulliamy, as late as May of 2002, just a couple of months ago, would your opinion as to the man whose authority you were given to penetrate Omarska and Trnopolje concentration camps in August of 1992 an ITN team would be Milan Kovacevic, true or false?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not his authority alone, but he was certainly part of the body as -- that was indicated to us that was giving us the authority. I don't know what authority or what the -- as it were the relationship of authority or power was between the top official and his deputy or, as I think they were presented to us, introduced to us, the president and the vice-president. If it was Mr. Kovacevic who was, as I said before and I'm going over this, was doing most of the talking at the meeting, then that's probably what I meant by that. But I don't really, and I'm going to sort of stick with this, we were asking all of them as a body to go at various points of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a little more precise than that. Isn't it true, sir, that in May of 2002, you wrote an article which related to this Tribunal and specifically were giving an overview of what you called a "blue chair" upon which you testified from and gave a synopsis of what you thought witnesses may or may not say in the Milosevic trial, and then you gave your readers a little background about your experience and you identify yourself? I'm not done. I'm just pausing for the interpreters. Sorry. And you further identify yourself as being a person who had testified in cases before the Tribunal, among others against Milan Kovacevic, and then you proceed to say: "Milan Kovacevic, the man on whose authority I penetrated Omarska and Trnopolje concentration camps in August 1992 with an ITN team"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was the man on whose authority we went to the camps. He was the deputy president of the authority, the body who I was given to believe was in charge of the camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At no time in any of the articles that you, sir, wrote, whether they be the article of August 7, 1992, the article from February 1996, or the article in May of 2002 do you ever identify Dr. Milomir Stakic as the man upon whose authority you were able to penetrate Omarska or Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The article from which I'm quoting, do you regularly produce articles for this publication?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which publication?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the Bosnian Institute. It's called the Bosnian Report published by the Bosnian Institute?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not written an article for the Bosnian Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, may I tender a copy to the usher and she can distribute it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be DPD3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I have to admit for the record, if I may, we did actually mark, and I'm directing it to the Court as well as the OTP, the area on which we're focusing. It's underlined with an asterisk on the right side. Just so the record is clear, that's my indication. I didn't have a clean copy, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, just let me know what you've had an opportunity to look at the article, and I will have a couple of questions in connection with it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
