utterances.text: I have got the article in front of me. I remember it and I was slightly confused when you said May 2002, because I wrote this article quite a long time before that, in, I think, February 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can read it on the last page that this article was published in the Observer on the 7th of February, 2002. Evidently it's a reprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, on the top right hand portion it is a series of articles that appear in this Bosnian Institute or Bosnian Report, and the series is from January through May 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote the article during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you, if I may, still on this issue of control, when you left the meeting or were asked to leave the meeting of August 5, 1992, you stated that there was a debate among its members. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you and all the other international press, if you will, were asked to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked -- yes. We were all asked to wait outside while they talked on their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never came back to the municipal building or back in that room to have further discussions with either Dr. Stakic or any of the other individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, who was the individual who then, after this debate, advised you that they would take you to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what the debate was about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but Mr. Drljaca indicated to the ITN interpreter that they'd been discussing what to do with us and had come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Discussing or debating?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took it that the -- shall I say the argument between Mr. Arsic and others as to whether Manjaca was a suitable destination or not and whether we could or couldn't, should or shouldn't go to Manjaca had continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 35 of yesterday's transcript you also tell us while waiting outside and discussing with Mr. Simo Drljaca the results of this debate or discussion that a reporter came and wanted to join your group from Zagreb, I believe, from see and discover Omarska. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, help me with this with respect to who would give whom permission to go to the camp? I think you said that the reporter was asked if he had permission from Dr. Karadzic or any other members' authority to go to Omarska. I think -- that's a long question. I'm sorry. Just trying to give you a little background on it. And I think you then said that Simo Drljaca asked him: "Did you get the authority from Radovan Karadzic?" The answer was no. Therefore, he wasn't allowed to join you and other members of ITN; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was asked, as I recall, whether he was part of Dr. Karadzic's party or some such phrase. I don't think the actual word "permission from" Dr. Karadzic, but it was his party, the part of, as it were, the organised tour, if you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your impression that Dr. Karadzic was merely organising a tour for the international press, correct, but not authorising them to go to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was my impression that Dr. Karadzic had issued a form of challenge. And I'm sorry if I didn't make this clear yesterday, when he was in London that allegations about Omarska were not true and that he would make the necessary arrangements for us to go. It wasn't a tour for the international press. In fact, the ejection of Mr. Juda from the convoy I think showed that's exactly what it wasn't. It was a specific -- these were specific arrangements for ITN and ourselves to go to Omarska and that what was going on was the realisation of those arrangements despite the obstacles I've discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe, as you sit here, that Mr. Juda, who came from Zagreb, would have been able to merely call up Dr. Kovacevic or talk to Simo Drljaca and obtain authority to go on to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That calls for speculation. The witness can testify about the facts of how he received permission, about what he observed, but it doesn't serve any purpose to have him speculate about someone else's -- what might have happened and under another circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know since you were there, Mr. Vulliamy, whether or not you gave the advice to this reporter that all he had to do was call Drljaca or Kovacevic and he'd be able to go see Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't give that advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if -- do you know, sir, if the reporter himself asked Drljaca for permission to be able to go see the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, we spoke a little bit earlier at the beginning of the cross about three concepts, one being your actual contemporaneous notes, then your aide-memoirs, as you call them, and ultimately the end result of your interview compiling both your contemporaneous notes, your aide-memoirs and your recollection of the events which is the final product, an article hopefully; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for this case, did you at any time prepare this aide-memoire or type out a summary of the minutes from the August 5, 1992 meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparation for this case, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In preparation -- or at any time for any reason had you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I prepare typewritten notes, yes. I think you know. They're in a file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't, and I just want to make sure it's clear. I'm not talking about the February 1996 typewritten aide-memoirs. I'm asking, from the August 5, 1992 notes that you have, whether or not you have prepared any aide-memoires?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from August the 5th. No. There was no way of typing stuff at that. I wrote the article longhand and it was dictated. I didn't have equipment of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the August 5, 1992 article, you went from contemporaneous notes to the ultimate article; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Contrasting that with the February 1996 interview, you actually had all three: Contemporaneous notes, aide-memoires, and then the ultimate and final article; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I can explain. In 1992, there was no means of transmitting, no technical means, at least not available to me, of transmitting material from any sort of computer or electronic device. There were -- I think people might know there were problems in -- at the time. In 1996, I went from Prijedor to Zagreb and did prepare typewritten notes because I did have access to a computer in Zagreb and prepared typewritten notes on the basis of consultations with my colleague and with the translator. I think I've explained that the shorthand that I've read out, and I'm sure you can hear, is not -- it's not an exact, it's not a fluent account of things. In fact, if you were to quote from the shorthand direct, you'd make most people sound like inarticulate idiots, which none of these people are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just, for the purpose of cleaning up a couple of things, ask the Court if you can distribute relevant portions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the book "Seasons in Hell" by Ed Vulliamy that we discussed, specifically pages 8 and 9 and pages 100 and 101?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed. This would be DPD4, and may I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, it was already number DPD2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this hint. Now, what I wanted to state, the witness might please direct our -- yes, show us indeed parts of the book if in case he believes that these parts my be, of course not deliberately, out of content and that some other portions of your book would be helpful or would assist the Tribunal in coming closer to the truth. So therefore, please don't hesitate to draw our attention to other parts of your book if you feel necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour. I haven't seen the book for a good many years, but I will do the best I can from my recollection, but I'm very grateful and thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would request, if there is no objection from the Defence and if Your Honour -- I believe that the -- regarding pages 100 -- I think counsel said 100 and 101, the visit to the Omarska camp, as I found it in the book, begins on page 98, going through page 107, and I have copies for everyone of those pages, those ten pages if that's acceptable. Except that, since I did the copying and not Ms. Karper, the staple is in the wrong part of the page. So I have the copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we have concurrent contribution, but it shouldn't be a problem. No objections by the Defence. Let the OTP tender this -- what was it, ten pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: From page 98 to 107, ten pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if we also hear the other part, it always assists us, and therefore, could you be so kind and distribute also these parts. So these pages, starting with Chapter 5, would be DP8. Any additional pages? It is not the case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You can never anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is just a little housekeeping matter, Mr. Vulliamy, by think the Court asked you a question. I'm not sure if you have answered it or if you would like the opportunity to answer it. I'll certainly give that to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the moment. Let's deal with the matter now, and if there are other -- if there are other issues then I'll bring them up, but, please, I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it accurate as it's reflected on pages 8 and 100 -- strike that. Is it accurate in your book as reflected on page 8 and page 100 that it is Dr. Kovacevic who is the man who is in charge of and responsible for the Omarska and Trnopolje camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the -- that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the impression we were given at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at any time during this meeting that you had on August 5, 1992, did Colonel Arsic ever introduce the international press, as I've coined you that attended it meeting, did he ever introduce Dr. Stakic as the man who was in charge of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He indicated that the civilian authorities were the authorities on whose authority, pardon the repetition, on whose authority we would need if we were to go into the camps, and by that he indicated, and I think also said, three people in the room, Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic, and Mr. -- And Colonel, sorry, Arsic -- forgive me, and the police chief Simo Drljaca. And as I've said before and it's -- there's material here and there's material in what I said yesterday, it was Kovacevic who was doing most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And seemed to be, if you like, the most hands-on character in the room, if you'll pardon the expression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at no time would you have written that in 1992, Dr. Stakic was introduced to us as the man who was in charge of Omarska. This was said by Colonel Vladimir Arsic. If you were quoted somewhere as that, would you consider that to be an embellishment, a distortion, or an outright lie?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Vladimir Arsic ever pointed to Mr. Stakic and said, "This is the man in charge of Omarska." I don't think I've said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you and that's okay, but if you did, what would you qualify it as being, an embellishment, a distortion, or a lie?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's ambiguous, because he just indicated he never said Dr. Arsic -- excuse me, Colonel Arsic pointed to Stakic and said, "This is the man." And counsel had earlier asked another question, so I'm not sure what the answer's directed to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow the objection, but I could clean it up if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Vulliamy, at any time write that "In 1992, Dr. Stakic was introduced to us as the man who was in charge of Omarska. This was said by Colonel Vladimir Arsic." Just those two sentences. Did you ever write or make that statement to anyone?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that when you did your aide-memoires and shipped the aide-memoires to the OTP, specifically Michael Keegan, that in fact that's the first thing you write in summarising your report with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's fair to say that Dr. Stakic was the senior official --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please give the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was the senior official, the top man, in the group of people in the room on whose authority we went to Omarska and whose authority we were told by Colonel Arsic we would need to go to Omarska or at least to complete the last phase of Dr. Karadzic's arrangements for us. Why I have written the -- the position of Mr. Kovacevic in overseeing the running of the camps is because after that meeting, when the -- what I call the circus, the press, descended on Omarska and Trnopolje in the days following, Mr. Kovacevic, in a number of television and newspaper interviews, was put up as the man or the front man answering for the authority running those camps to give their comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that being the debate that occurred on August 5th, 1992, do you know what position, if any, Dr. Milomir Stakic had in connection with the decisions or discussion that is were taking place while you were outside?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I know is that as a group, the three of them presumably changed their minds or were told to change their minds or came to a decision that we would be able to continue to Omarska to see the little that we saw. This and this but not that, whatever it was, and then to proceed to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Dr. Stakic, when you met with him in February 1992, as to whether or not he had any control or authorisation with respect to the detention camp Omarska or Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if you could wait for just a second. I believe counsel misspoke, and I believe he meant February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about if we do it this way, Mr. Vulliamy: How about if I first pass out with the Court's permission what I've identified as aide-memoirs from the contemporaneous notes of the February 1996 meeting, okay?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's okay so long as they're not presented as only coming from the contemporaneous notes. Another colleague of mine had taken his notes as well, and there were consultations with the translator as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we're passing this out, the other colleague was Roger who from The New York Times?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said his name and I'm not sure if it's appropriate, but you've asked me, and it's Roger Cohen from The New York Times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: DPD4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if you see on the top of that Exhibit DPD4, it has your name, and then you proceed in the first sentence of this four-page document to state the following: "In 1992, Dr. Stakic was introduced to us as the man who was in charge of Omarska. This was said by Colonel Vladimir Arsic, local army commander ..." And then it goes on. End quote. My question was earlier, is this your aide-memoire, as you called it, from the meeting of February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and the sentence you've just quoted, it was aide-memoire to myself, and that was not as you're not tired of reminding me, that was not published and it refers to the fact that he was in charge of the authority on whose authority we went to Omarska, mainly the authorities of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm getting a little tired but not that tired. In connection with this, this is the actual aide-memoire that you sent to the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent a disk with -- of this material to the -- to the Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is -- what I'm asking you is that sentence where you claim to the OTP that Dr. Stakic was the man in charge of Omarska, now knowing what you wrote in August of 1992, reviewing parts of your book of February 1994, your testimony here today and yesterday, would you consider this statement to be, since we know now Dr. Arsic did not actually tell you that Dr. Stakic was the man in charge of Omarska, would this sentence be considered an embellishment, distortion, or lie?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I object because the question, although it referred to the sentence, only quoted -- excuse me. I withdraw the objection. It was the next sentence I was -- sorry. I missed a period. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't catch your answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This isn't in quotation marks, and I'm going to stand by my -- by my -- by -- by what it means, that he's in charge of the -- of the authorities on whose authority we went to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's neither an embellishment, nor distortion, nor a lie in your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you read these contemporaneous notes of this meeting that you had with Dr. Stakic in 1992 obviously we didn't see the questions, I think the OTP covered the fact that you would not have pre-written questions incorporated within your contemporaneous notes taking, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read those minutes to us early this morning commencing at 9.30. I didn't note anywhere in the contemporaneous notes or your direct examination that during the meeting of February 1996 you had a discussion with Dr. Stakic about The Hague and the International Crime Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Am I correct in that summary?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- think I we did mention The Hague, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Kovacevic, for sure. I'm not sure about Dr. Stakic. We might have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've read the transcript and I beg to differ, but if you look on the page of this exhibit, DPD4, I think it's the third page?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second page. Thank you. You found the section which is in the top half of the page 2 of DPD4. You claim that you asked Dr. Stakic "if you're worried about The Hague", and then you proceed to give a description or a summary, if you will, of what he said. Now, when I compare that to the contemporaneous notes, there seems to be many inconsistencies with what that portion of your contemporaneous notes are and that is which is reflected in the handwritten notes. My question to you and I'm sure you recall that in 1998, you also admitted and acknowledged that there were numerous inconsistencies with the contemporaneous notes and your aide-memoire as it related to Dr. Kovacevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're calling this a transcript. It's not a transcript. And I can answer, if I may, two questions -- your two questions, because I didn't get the chance to answer the first one. I -- noting this, yes, I do see there's a question about the Hague. If my memory serves me, which it -- I mean, I don't think I asked about the Hague. Mr. Cohen may have asked about the Hague. I didn't mention it this morning because, as you can see, the reply and certainly the notes that I took and read out this morning don't deal much with The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hang on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Because the second sentence of that sentence actually does have the word Hague in it and that second sentence you attribute what Dr. Stakic said. If you look at the second line "Whoever did that should be worried about the Hague." So how could you tell us here now, today, that in the answer Dr. Stakic never used the word The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel, in all seriousness, to let the witness speak out before interrupting the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do say here that this is a -- that if it's here, he would have mentioned The Hague. This -- these notes were compiled by myself and my colleague after consultations with the translator. And actually, he has -- when he's talking about this, he has rather a good point about the expulsion of Serbs from the Krajina, and whoever did that should be worried about The Hague. Quite so. That isn't in my notes. I think, and I haven't got them here, but I think I recall a note saying one and a half million Serb, with an arrow pointing, which would be an arrow pointing towards Mr. Cohen, it having been his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the usher please provide the witness once again with these notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. On the second page, which in the pencil mark I've got is DP6-2 about halfway down it says: "One and a half M Serbs," with an arrow pointing to the left, to the right. Pardon me. That's where my colleague was sitting, and that would be perhaps a question that he wanted answered, and I did not have any record of that in my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was something that you recall and then incorporated in your aide-memoires and sent to the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, it was something that I didn't recall, it was something that from what I can gather from the way this is laid out would have been in my colleague's notes. Although we do pick up in my notes, and I -- if I can preempt you, there's a mistake, great-grandfather and grandfather which I observe immediately, but my notes do pick up with his family history, which I found to be interesting and, indeed, telling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get back to that in the February 1996 meeting in a few minutes. I just want to try to conclude, and I'm endeavouring to conclude the April 5, 1992 meeting, if you could believe it. With respect to gaining authorisation to go to the Omarska and Trnopolje detention centres, were you or any representatives from the ITN crew --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is August the 5th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Everyone's correcting me on that. Thank you. August 5, 1992, did you obtain written permission from anyone to go to the Omarska and Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. I wish we had. We didn't. It was, as I think I sort of outlined yesterday, it was quite a struggle to get there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you. You were in the meeting at the municipal building for approximately, I think you said, one and a half to two hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that. I don't know exactly how long, but it was a long meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you tell me. I don't want to use any numbers --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one and a half to two hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the trip from the municipal building to the actual Omarska Detention Centre was how long? Twenty-five minutes I think you said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a little more forty-five, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forty-five minutes. How long did you stay at the Omarska Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say an hour or a little longer, most of which was in this office building, office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is where you also had a meeting with, among others, Simo Drljaca, Colonel Arsic, and Mr. Meakic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Colonel Arsic was there. At the meeting, it was certainly Mr. Drljaca, certainly Mr. Meakic the commander, and the Major Milutinovic from Banja Luka was also with us, but I don't think Colonel Arsic. But there was a meeting there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time did Dr. Milomir Stakic accompany you to the Omarska Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither the president nor his deputy came on the actual convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then after spending the hour or longer at the Omarska Detention Centre, you proceeded to go to Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, as recounted yesterday. Initially against our -- against our wishes. We wanted to stay in Omarska, and as you know we weren't allowed to and we were rather bundled off to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you spend at Trnopolje, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One and a half hours, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Dr. Stakic at any time accompany you or any members of the ITN crew to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the same convoy as had set off from Prijedor minus, I think, Major Milutinovic who peeled off at some point. I can't remember when.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know from your background you do not have a criminal justice or a police academy degree, and you're not experienced in that, but do you know, sir, what the authority or hierarchy was in the police, the MUP, M-U-P, in Prijedor municipality in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That calls for speculation. There would be no basis for him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact hierarchy. I was given to believe that because of the -- what was seen as the extreme situation in the area, the -- whatever arrangements had been provisionally suspended and that this group, staff, committee, or whatever, had been formed, and I was also given to believe by Colonel Arsic that he was the military wing of that and that the other three gentlemen were the civilian wing of that, and if the MUP did not come under the -- the civilian command, then I don't know because I doubt they were a totally independent body. But the answer is I don't know the exact chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification of the record on this page, when speaking about group, staff, committee, you always have in mind crisis group, Crisis Staff, or Crisis Committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's specifically Messrs. Stakic, Kovacevic, Drljaca and Arsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn, sir, for the first time because I duly note in your August 7th, 1992 publication, article in the February 1996 contemporaneous notes as well as the aide-memoires that we have before us, when do you start identifying them in any form as being members of a "Crisis Committee" or group or staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why, if it's true, that in fact these people were introduced as being members of the Crisis Committee that word or those words, group, staff, committee, never appear in either your contemporaneous notes, your articles from 1992, your contemporaneous notes or your aide-memoires and articles of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they probably do appear somewhere but I thought they were called the Crisis Committee or I said, I think, a number of times if it's staff I'll stand corrected, but committee is the word I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've read into the record your actual contemporaneous notes from 1992 and 1996. Do you recall ever identifying them as such?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the notes. They're introduced there as colonel, president, and vice-president as I recollect. I don't have the notes in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your article of August 7th, 1992, which you had the opportunity to rereview, do you note whether you identify this group or committee or staff and the members of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly. There were -- after that day, there were perhaps other things that seemed more relevant than the label. I think I do, and I've now just noticed that I or in the editing Mr. Kovacevic has been wrongly labelled as the president, but I don't think I used that term, no, and I would ask perhaps yourself, the Court, to understand that after finding those places and after trying to wonder what was in the place we hadn't seen, I -- forgive me if the label was left out. As you observed, it wasn't in the notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recall, you testified after the visit to Omarska and Trnopolje, you proceeded directly to Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We might have stopped for a -- some sort of snack, but I don't -- I mean, if it was, it was brief. We went back to Belgrade that night, arrived late or in the early hours of the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while in Belgrade, the following two or three days that you were there, you had an opportunity, as you said, to have tea with vice-president Professor Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to talk to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in Pale he had walked past us while we were having lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't talk to him in Belgrade but you talked to him in Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to him, no. There was a brief rising, sitting down again, but no discussion, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know there was no discussion or do you recall anything he may have said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything he may have said, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me direct your attention to the sworn testimony you gave on June 7, 1996, in the Dusko Tadic trial, which commences on page 1455, line 31 and 32, and then your answer proceeds on page 1456, lines 1 through 4 in particular, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me read this in the record, Your Honour and then ask the witness a question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As follows:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction from the Bosnian Serb leadership to the reports you published and TV coverage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pretty explosive reaction all around. The Bosnian Serb leadership said various things. General Mladic, as I recall, said that the pictures had been transmitted were forgeries and photo montages or else pictures showing Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps. Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please proceed to the end of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember Dr. Karadzic's exact words but they suggested that there had been some exaggeration. I think they suggested that he was surprised by what had been discovered while it was, forgive me, it was the Yugoslav president Milan Panic who said that anybody running such places would be punished and that they should be closed down.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you asked me if I remember giving that testimony. I don't actually remember saying those exact words, but it looks to make sense to me, and I'm -- I do -- I'm sure I was asked what the reaction was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here do you recall General Mladic saying that the pictures were forgeries and photo montages and they were pictures showing Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that being reported, yes. I when I -- you asked me if I'd met him. He didn't say it directly to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember also with respect to Omarska the conversation with Major Milutinovic wherein he told you: "How can there be anything wrong in Omarska?" This is in February 1996 when you visited him. "How can there be anything wrong in Omarska in August 1992? The journalists went to Omarska in 1992 and they found nothing. I bite my tongue." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir: Who other than General Mladic, as you recall, and Major Colonel Milutinovic made the statement with respect to there being nothing being wrong in Omarska and that photos were forgeries or montages which may be depicting Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And many others, actually. It's been said a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the Dusko Tadic trial, you can find the fact that no one other than the individuals you identify in those transcripts actually made this summary statement that they were photo montages or that they were forgeries or that they were Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe -- objection. I believe it's an unfair question since the question that was quoted from the Tadic trial was "What was the reaction of the Bosnian Serb leadership." I don't think it's fair to include the mayor of a town as the leadership of the Bosnian Serb entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would leave aside this conclusion. No doubt the answer starts "The Bosnian Serb leadership said various things." Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at your aide-memoire, DPD4, page 2, bottom of the page, you seem to attribute that exact same quote to Dr. Stakic, do you not? In fact, you even add: "Bite tongue." Almost verbatim to the language that you attribute and you were reaction to what Major Milutinovic said during your sworn testimony in the Dusko Tadic case, specifically appearing on page 1464.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, yeah. When people say something to the effect of there was nothing wrong in Omarska in August 1992, the journalists found nothing, or in this case they were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps, I it's more than just an expression of speech. Yeah, "Bite tongue," or cheek. I felt like -- I'd learned and seen an awful lot between then and now, now being February 1996, in that war. And when I'm told, "Oh, you should have been there," or something to that effect, I do feel like saying, "Well, excuse me, I was, and I was with the crew that shot those pictures of supposed Serbs in Muslim camps, and they were not." But in the interests of carrying on the conversation and especially given the circumstances I think I explained earlier, not, as it were, playing my hand on the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in 1996, during the Dusko Tadic trial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- You discussed the interview you had with Dr. Stakic in February of 1996, and you were asked precisely the question with respect to what his reaction was relating to the pictures that were shown on TV in 1992. At that time, under oath, you stated, page 1463, line 27 through 33, and it proceeds to the next page, Your Honour, you state: "I do not actually recall. I think that the man introduced as the lawyer butted in at one point and said, 'oh, they were forgeries.' And I think Dr. Stakic mumbled something about them being Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps. It was clear that this whole conversation was being taped. He started messing around with the tape recorder, and then it became clear that the man who had started off as the deputy, who then became the lawyer, was some sort of policeman or bodyguard, and our interpreter had recognised him and was trying to convey this to us with sign language, pointing to the tape recorder." The next page it proceeds, just so I can have it in complete context for the OTP and the record on page 1464 line 1, "The conversation ended but we kept asking about Omarska, but the reply was always 'Jasenovac,' 'Jasenovac,' 'Jasenovac' so we were going around and around. We were asking about one lot of camps and the reply would be another lot of camps in the previous generation which I found interesting." You go on to say on line five: "We ended up, Dr. Stakic said, it was dark outside by now, he said 'it is very brave of you to be here with us at this time of night.' He took -- which we took as a good cue to make our way back to Banja Luka." In 1996 when you gave sworn testimony, you were unable to recall the reaction of Dr. Stakic. Today, based on your aide-memoires, you seem to have a clearer recollection. If you look, sir, specifically on the page of your contemporaneous notes, I'll direct your attention to DP6-3, which I believe the second portion of that correlates with this section of what you call your aide-memoires. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read that in the record today for us, sir. Does it anywhere within there talk about Dr. Stakic mumbling about something, "Serbs in Muslim camps," or "Muslims in Serb camps"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says they were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The television pictures of the Omarska camp about which he was being asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read further in those contemporaneous notes to identify exactly what it is that this context in your contemporaneous notes is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says as a journalist you have to come on the spot. They were never being collected. Omarska -- it's clear we're talking about Omarska. And then he says there was only an interrogation process for a particular number of Muslims and so on. We're -- we're talking about, and it's perfectly clear to me and it was then, we're talking about Omarska, and we're talking about the ITN pictures of Omarska. You've asked me if I may say respectfully, many, many questions, unless you're simply reading my statements onto the record about this discussion of this interview in other cases. This is one of the instances, including the tongue-biting business. To me it is perfectly clear, as I recall it being perfectly clear at the time to Dr. Stakic and his friend, that we were talking about Omarska in 1992. We were talking about the footage of Omarska in 1992. And I could be pardoned for saying there'd been an awful lot of these sort of remarks, including those of the leadership, that we heard earlier. And in my own country, the denial of these camps was becoming ubiquitous and it -- I was not happy to hear it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, immediately within the contemporaneous notes, Dr. Stakic proceeds to discuss, as you've read into the record, the type of individuals that were detained in Omarska camp. So reconcile for me how on one hand they would say A, they don't exist, but in the very next line, the very next sentence of your contemporaneous notes, Dr. Stakic is discussing and trying to explain the individuals who were detained at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I think he was negating himself. I think he was saying two different things at the same time. And that is not the only time one has heard that sort of argument. I repeat. It was clear to me then and clear to me now that whether he says they were pictures of Serbs in Muslim camps, we were talking about the pictures of Omarska about which we were talking, and then he said -- he goes on to say that there were some sorts of inmates held at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I recognise that your testimony is that it was clear to you today -- or it was clear to you in 1992, 1996, and it's clear to you today, but on June 7, 1996, you, under oath, said you actually don't recall and that it wasn't clear to you as to who made the statement. In fact, at that time, under both, you clearly state that Dr. Stakic was interrupted by this other gentleman that you previously identified and that the other gentleman, according to your sworn testimony on June 6, 1996, used the word "forgery." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Argumentative. The witness has given the answers to the questions already stated. Counsel is simply arguing his view that it's inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this, Mr. Vulliamy, if you may. During August 5th, 1992 and the article that appeared on August 7th, 1992, did you do any follow-up interviews or have any conversations with Dr. Milomir Stakic other than the February 1996 interview that we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you expect Dr. Stakic to read your article and to give a commentary on as you did for Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wasn't this a misleading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think earlier in his -- if I may explain. I think Mr. Vulliamy earlier said that he wrote an article and that he didn't get a letter or an objection from Dr. Kovacevic on the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because he didn't send this article to Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking that just now about Dr. Stakic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be better to put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you send the article or in any way correspond to Dr. Stakic relating to the events that you published on August 7th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And by the way, the article was very widely circulated at the time, translated, and indeed displayed across television screens, which is not something I'm particularly proud of but it just happened to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to this meeting of August 5th, 1992. Do you remember, sir, during this hour and a half or two-hour meeting that in fact you were so uptight with the fact that you weren't taken immediately to Omarska camp that you turned your back on the people who were welcoming you there and ignored completely this tape or video that the hosts were trying to share and show you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about turning my back on them, but if there is some pictorial evidence of me expressing my displeasure at this continuing obfuscation, then I wouldn't be surprised. I think that comes across quite clearly in my book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who got the video in order that it be played for the ITN and the international press that was there. Who went and obtain the video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought tape into the room and put it in the video player and played the tape?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who physically put the cassette in the video player, but it was Mr. Kovacevic who gave the sort of commentary and the presentation. As regards the book, by the way, I'm not sure that Mr. Stakic's authority, and Your Honour kindly gave me opportunity to make reference to the book, I believe counsel have it, I don't, and haven't seen, it but I'm not quite sure that there might not be some other reference or the reference to Mr. Stakic being the mayor is the only one in the book, but obviously it rather than I can be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Judges are in the same position as you in this common law setting where the Judges have no, yes, possibility first to review the documents for the -- in preparation of the hearing. But maybe it can be of assistance when making a reference back. And if you identify something in your book even after your testimony, it could be helpful, if you would send or draw our attention by sending a letter to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, and I'm sorry to interrupt the proceedings. The thought just occurred to take you up on your offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You don't interrupt. You assist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, assist me with this, sir, if you don't mind, Mr. Vulliamy. As you sit here, do you recall at any time in your book whether or not you mention that Dr. Stakic held any other position other than mayor of the Prijedor municipality on or about August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but I'm not sure if that reference that you've picked out is the only one. It may be. I'm just -- I just haven't seen it for a very long time. And if it is, so be it. If it's not, then perhaps that should be looked at. That's all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to a different area, but with the guidance of the Court. I'd like to discuss with you the February 1996 meeting that you had with both Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic. Although I think I might be no more than an hour and a half, it may be prudent or at least I would suggest that it is, in order that we're more efficient to end the proceedings now, unless the Court would rather that we proceed with the questioning with respect to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think we have any time to lose, and I would ask the Defence to proceed for another 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to your meeting and interview with Dr. Kovacevic in February of 1996, you write both in your contemporaneous notes and in your aide-memoires that you shared with Dr. Kovacevic a bottle of homemade brandy, namely slivovitz; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the whole bottle, but the best part of it was consumed, in the most part by himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in reading his notes into the record there, sir, did you read anywhere within your contemporaneous notes that, in fact, Dr. Kovacevic, during the interview that you were conducting of him, drank the better part of this bottle of whiskey?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. It was not whiskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was hoping the translators would correct me. Slivovitz. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there might be some indentations, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read from your contemporaneous notes today. I don't recall it. I do note in your aide-memoires that you do actually make reference to the time of the meeting and ultimately when it is that Dr. Kovacevic drank these seven or eight shots of slivovitz during your meeting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be about right. I'd say he had seven or eight. And Mr. Cohen and I and the translator would have had one each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's true, as you testified in the Keraterm proceedings, last June 2001, that Dr. Kovacevic, during that meeting, having consumed seven to eight good-sized shots of homemade brandy, that he was at the very least in no condition to drive, and you could not conclude that he was sober?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I said "good-sized". Not sort of full glasses but shots, yes. And certainly by the standards of -- I do recall being asked the question, and certainly by the standards of the laws which I hope pertain to this country, he would not be in a fit state to drive. Having slivovitz in the morning was perhaps not as uncommon in the war and in that part of the world as it might seem to people here. In fact, when you're in the trenches as I was, I used to start the day reasonably frequently with something with a shot to warm the body and soul and as did many of the soldiers. Certainly seven was a lot, but I wouldn't want to -- yes. He was not sober for sure, but I wouldn't want that to be interpreted perhaps by the rather more puritanical standards that we would use.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wars and in these circumstances, people tend to have a drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in 1996, February; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the war, granted, but I'm making a general point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to know is what your journalistic obligations, were to interview a man, after having met with Michael Keegan and the OTP on at least two prior occasions within the six-month period prior to your meeting, what your obligations are to continue to conduct an interview with a man who is obviously intoxicated.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My journalistic obligations were to my editor and my newspaper and to the assignment that I had been given to go back and interview and talk to these people if I could. I didn't know that I would. And if Dr. Kovacevic chose to have more than the share of drink around the table, that's his decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, at no time did you think that you were taking advantage of that interview process by continuing to ask him questions and having him drink and become intoxicated before your very eyes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say intoxicated. I said not sober. He was talking coherently, albeit in a fairly haunted way, and the answer to your question is no, given the gravity of what was being discussed, his apparent willingness, I would say eagerness, to talk. He said at one point, "This is more relaxing than my professional problems." And the owns is no. We were dealing with a matter of extremely serious nature. We were talking about the deaths of very large numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people, in your mind, at that time were you discussing with Dr. Kovacevic involving deaths in the Prijedor, Bosnia area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, irrelevant of what he thought at that time about the number of people who died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you, in your article following the interview that you had with Dr. Kovacevic and the series that you were producing subsequent to the meetings that you had with Dr. Stakic and Dr. Kovacevic, did you note in that article at any time that Dr. Kovacevic was "Not sober"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what words I used. I might have said drunk. You said intoxicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go with whatever -- do you want to go with not sober, drunk, or intoxicated? Any of the three is acceptable?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's agree that they're all pretty near the point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may remind the parties to pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your meeting with Dr. Kovacevic, did you at any time tell him that you were a witness or potential witness that was soon to testify, actually within four months, in the Dusko Tadic trial which took place, as we know, during the month of June 1996, and that you were actually investigating to fulfil an obligation you made to the OTP relating to the factors of systematic and widespread pattern in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think journalistically and ethically and morally that you had an obligation when interviewing someone about such serious matters as you've described that you at the very least had the obligation to tell him the purpose for your interview?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the interview was to publish an article. And I did introduce myself as a member of the press although I did not give my name because it was reasonably well known in the area, and I didn't consider it prudent for my own safety to give my name because I was in the area without permission, and I -- but I think if you're writing down notes and the person knows you're from the press, it's a reasonable assumption that you're going to write an article about what they say. At no point was -- did Dr. Kovacevic say that what he was saying was off the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with The New York Times editor by the name of David Binder?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you want to ask the question before I make the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was the question. I think I got an answer, but I'll check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's the next one I think I'm waiting for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said Roger Cohen was also an individual who accompanied you during these meetings and he was also from the New York Times; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this with the Court's permission, would you be surprised to find that an editor of the New York Times would not only be shocked but totally disappointed that had a journalist would breach their ethics and morality in conducting interviews with individuals while not identifying them and not sharing with them the actual true purpose for those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I have the basis, Your Honour? Because during -- if I may just reply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the questioning of numerous witnesses within the Prosecution's case in chief we were criticised by the OTP for not putting our case as they call it and I think the Court will that Ms. Joanna Korner made that argument quite eloquently and asked that we put our case to each of the witnesses. I don't understand the objection that counsel made. I apologise for that. I don't understand the ruling and would merely like for purposes of the record to have a complete understanding of both the objection and the ruling if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The basis is the counsel cannot interject an opinion by someone who is not called as a witness simply as a way to get that before the Court and ask a witness would he be surprised to hear that. When the Defence witnesses testify, I will not read to them opinions that I receive from other witnesses, from experts regarding the war in Bosnia and say, "Would you be surprised to learn this?" And it's an improper question and counsel knows that. He wouldn't be able to do that in the United States and he can't do that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have covered this area enough, and we have heard the opinion that the witness told us quite clearly that he had no ethical problems emanating from the points you made, and I have also to mention that I was liberal enough to allow your question, once again trying to confuse the purpose of this interviewing Mr. Kovacevic, namely when you mentioned in one sentence this special task and at the same time making a link to a meeting or discussion with representatives of the OTP. The witness has clearly stated there was no such link. And it is for the witness, and we have heard the witness's opinion, and he didn't identify any obstacles to proceed the way he did. There might be other opinions on this issue, and this is true whenever specialists, be it lawyers, be it journalists or whomsoever, they have different opinions on these issues, and we should be more than glad that we have different opinions. So therefore, it doesn't make sense to answer this question. Therefore, the question is not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I can just clarify the point with respect to specifically the nexus, if you will, between Mr. Vulliamy and the OTP, and if I can just put this question to him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, when you interviewed Dr. Stakic, at that time you knew you were going to be a witness in the Dusko Tadic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not to say there was a nexus between me and the OTP any more than there's a nexus between any witness and the -- they didn't call it the OTP then so far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My point is I'm removing that equation. All I'm asking you is whether or not you knew by conducting the interview of Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic you knew that you were going to be a witness in the Dusko Tadic trial four months later.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I hadn't actually received a summons, but I'd had the meetings and I was aware that it was, if not extremely likely, that I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you discussed with Dr. Kovacevic at least, Dusko Tadic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he brought up Dusko Tadic. But certainly The Hague and indeed the case came into the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At no time while Dr. Kovacevic may have brought it up or yourself, at no time did you inform him to say that you are a witness that is soon to testify in the Tadic trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At no time did I tell him I was to testify. And if my memory serves me, he -- he introduced Dusko Tadic by way of making a distinction between people who had actually killed other people and people who hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Roger Cohen who was also at that time with The New York Times have a discussion as to whether or not you should honestly inform the individuals that are interviewing of both your status and the purpose of your interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think -- I think we have covered this area already this morning and now it's exhausted, and it's not for the Defence counsel to blame a witness on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I could ask the question. I'm not sure if I understand, respectfully, your ruling. I'm not putting blame. All I asked was, if I may, whether or not Mr. Vulliamy had a conversation with the other reporter who was there, Roger Cohen, and I identified him just for the record as being specifically from The New York Times. I don't believe that we've covered that. I'm not trying to blame the witness for having that discussion or not having the discussion, because I don't know if they had it or they didn't have it. So forgive me for asking an inarticulate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is related to the entire line of questions you put now and you put already this morning, and I think this area is really covered. We heard the answers of the witness twice, and therefore, any additional questions on this issue would be more than repetitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move now to this area with Dr. Stakic, specifically the interview. I think it would be prudent, I think because some of the questions have been perhaps inarticulate and the Court has sustained numerous objections from the OTP if we finish at this point and reconvene tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As the parties know and I just asked for the time elapsed during examination-in-chief and cross-examination, taking in addition in account a huge part of the examination-in-chief was used for reading out the notes, the cross-examination should not cover more than 60 minutes tomorrow morning, and then there is time for re-examination and questions from the Judges and additional questions emanating from these questions for the next 30 minutes. So that we have to conclude the testimony after all in all 90 minutes tomorrow. And I would ask the registry to inform the witness for our next deposition to be taken that this deposition taking starts not earlier than 11.30. This concludes today's hearing if there are not mandatory contributions by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is one. If I could request permission. At the beginning of today's testimony, the witness indicated his concern about some confidential information, an address I believe he specifically said, on his notes if there is no objection, may I have permission, if the Defence does not object, to discuss this with the witness for five minutes, ten minutes now after we conclude Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We could go into private session. I think private session is enough for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could do that or I could discuss it privately and just report whether we have a problem or not. We may be able to resolve it between us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned it earlier and asked closed session. I think its it's not necessary. You know the efforts of a closed session in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, I ask kindly to go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
